#9757. Microsoft Debuts Offensive, Defensive Security Tools for the AI Era

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

At its Ignite technical conference, Microsoft announced AI agent security tools and transparency standards to protect enterprise systems.

At its annual Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft announced security initiatives to help customers secure artificial intelligence (AI) deployments and strengthen their security posture.

Executives touted tools that could discover and block agents running on employees' Windows devices, as well as the general availability of Perception, originally introduced in July as Project Perception and in public preview within Microsoft Defender since August. The "machine-speed" agentic security system simulates and detects attacks and protects everything from end-user PCs to cloud systems, the company said.

The company also unveiled an AI Transparency Initiative to develop standards for independently verifying AI behavior. More than 40 organizations will collaborate under this umbrella to develop open standards to make AI systems accountable, independently verifiable, and safe by design, regardless of model or provider.

Related:CrowdStrike Makes AI Security Push With Blockbuster Zscaler Deal

"At the end of the day, we believe there should never be a choice between innovation and safety. ... We are also working across the ecosystem to ensure that everyone can innovate with speed and scale safely," said Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella during a keynote speech on the first day of the conference.

During the opening-day keynote, Microsoft executives said advanced AI models are getting better at discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities. In November's Patch Tuesday, Microsoft fixed more than 1,000 vulnerabilities, compared with fewer than 100 in March.

Attacks and exploits are cheaper, easier, and more ubiquitous than ever before, said Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI.

"The last few months have really been, I think, a wake-up call and a warning shot for all of us," Suleyman said. "[That] means that agent security, alignment, and containment are going to be the most important things that we need to get right in 2027 and beyond."

To that end, Microsoft is stitching together existing tools to establish an end-to-end "trust" platform that controls AI agents in enterprises. Agent 365 maintains a registry of all AI agents in an enterprise, Entra gives agents their own identities and sandboxes to set boundaries, Purview governs data flows, and Defender detects and contains threats in real time.

System administrators can govern agents on an employee's PC, with new ways to stop unapproved agents, protect approved agents, and flag noncompliant devices. The platform also includes Perception, which protects corporate assets and environments with autonomous agentic AI tools. Red team agents simulate attacks, blue team agents detect attacks, and green team agents fix and remediate.

Related:Agentic Browsers Rewind Web Security by 20 Years

By connecting Windows with Agent 365, Entra, and Microsoft Perception, administrators can now discover 60 types of local agents on Windows devices, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot, while giving organizations new ways to restrict unapproved agents and protect approved ones with Intune and Microsoft Execution Containers, the company said.

"We're expanding the local agent types we can discover for a total of 65, including OpenClaw, OpenAI, Perplexity, and many more," said Yina Arenas, corporate vice president and chief product officer of identity and network access at Microsoft.

Perception is designed to protect against autonomous AI attacks, such as those carried out with open source penetration-testing tools like ARTEX. A pen-test red team agent can take the entire surface area of a Web application, including the authentication, APIs, injection attacks, and business logic, and create all of the evidence needed to confirm the app is not exploitable, Nadella said.

Microsoft officials at Ignite shared that the Windows endpoint security platform is reaching general availability on Windows 11, marking Microsoft's efforts to reduce reliance on kernel drivers.

Related:Agentic AI Challenges Progress in Confidential Computing

Windows baseline protection, now in preview, brings secure boot, virtualization-based security, memory integrity, and other protections into a single versioned security state, the company said. Baseline protection makes it easier for users and IT to understand whether a device is in a measurable security state to keep it up to date with the latest security safeguards and, when stronger assurance is required, verify that state through hardware-backed attestation, wrote Dana Huang, corporate vice president of Microsoft Security, on the company's blog. This will show up in an updated Windows Settings experience.

New vulnerability-shielding capabilities are designed to provide temporary protection for systems that can't yet be patched. Investments across Windows Autopatch, declarative management, and recovery help IT maintain intended state and restore operations. New Intune capabilities simplify application deployment, inventory, and life cycle management.

Microsoft is extending Intune and Windows Autopatch to eligible Windows Server scenarios, in preview, helping endpoint teams manage configuration, compliance, applications, updates, and security across Windows clients and supported servers, Huang said.

Microsoft's Integrated Security Operations Center and extended detection and response (XDR) core capabilities in Defender are now generally available. Organizations have access to more than 500 connectors, a built-in data lake, and 90 days of data retention at no extra cost.

Windows is also expanding post-quantum protection in the Windows TLS stack, including pure post-quantum key exchange and authentication.

Nadella also said the industry needs to come together on monitoring AI models and agents.

As part of the AI Transparency Initiative, Microsoft is working with organizations including Mastercard, Volvo Cars, KPMG, Adobe, and Accenture to define standards for AI transparency, security, and governance. Microsoft will apply those standards across its AI models and products, including development platform Microsoft Foundry and AI assistant Copilot.

Microsoft will also expand its collaboration in NIST's AI Agent Standards Initiative, which was established in February and focuses on the secure adoption of autonomous AI agents.

"We need standards that allow us to examine what AI sees and does, verify its actions independently, and control what it's allowed to do," Nadella said.

Agam Shah has covered enterprise IT for more than a decade. Outside of machine learning, hardware, and chips, he's also interested in martial arts and Russia.

AI companies are high-value targets for nation-state actors and cyber-espionage groups, but the recent Nvidia scandal shows the threats extend beyond the cyber realm.

#9755. Quantization-Aware Healing: a compressed, 4-bit model that outperforms its full-precision original

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

Our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it? We introduce Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH), and applied to a GPT-OSS 120B model compressed to 60B parameters and quantized to MXFP4, it produces a model that beats its own full-precision (bfloat16) version on 7 of 9 benchmarks. The 4-bit model ends up smaller, cheaper to run, and more accurate than the checkpoint it was quantized from. This inverts the usual relationship between a 4-bit model and the 16-bit model it came from.

Most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage. The difference between methods is entirely in that last step.

The dominant healing recipe is quantization-aware training (QAT). It inserts fake-quantization operators into the forward pass and keeps fine-tuning the model on a task loss, so the weights learn to tolerate the low-precision representation. In practice this means re-running an already expensive multi-stage post-training process, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, agentic tuning, through a noisier, lower-precision forward pass. It is costly, and as our results show, it can also become unstable if training continues too long past its best point.

An alternative, quantization-aware distillation (QAD), avoids re-running that history. Instead of a task loss, it distills a frozen full-precision teacher directly into the quantized student through a KL-divergence loss on the output logits. This works well when the only change is quantization, because a genuine full-precision version of the exact same model exists to act as teacher. But once a model has gone through structural compression, fewer layers, heads, or neurons, and not just fewer bits, that assumption breaks. There is no independently trained full-precision version of the smaller architecture. The only candidate teacher is the recovered bfloat16 checkpoint, which is itself a distilled approximation of the original model. Distilling from it anchors the quantized student to a degraded target and caps its accuracy at that recovered checkpoint's own ceiling.

So the question of how to heal a model that has been both structurally compressed and quantized was, until now, genuinely open.

QAH removes that ceiling with one change: it distills directly from the original, pre-compression model rather than from the recovered one. Teacher and student do not even share an architecture. The teacher is full-size and full-precision, the student is half the size and running in MXFP4. Because a teacher's output distribution is architecture-agnostic, nothing about the size or shape mismatch prevents the transfer. The student never sees hard labels, only the teacher's output distribution, matched through KL divergence on the logits.

This reframes what the quantization stage is doing. Under QAH it is no longer a lossy postprocessing step applied after healing is finished. It is a second, full pass of distillation against the original teacher, supervision that the bfloat16 checkpoint never received. The 4-bit student is not compensating for information lost to quantization; it is picking up information the earlier recovery stage did not have the time or data to transfer.

There is also a stability benefit that falls out of the loss itself. Because KL distillation ties the student to a fixed teacher distribution, once the student catches up there is no further pressure for it to drift. A cross-entropy task loss, by contrast, keeps pushing the student toward hard labels indefinitely. That difference turns out to matter for both accuracy and training stability, as the comparison below shows.

To make QAH work at long context, where the healing corpus includes documents up to 32k tokens, we reuse the memory-efficient chunked KL-divergence loss from our companion paper on efficient distillation. That loss computes the KL one slice of the sequence at a time and never materializes the full vocabulary-by-sequence grid, which is what makes 32k-token healing fit inside a fixed GPU memory budget. We covered the mechanics of that loss in a previous post.

QAH overview. After structural compression and quantization, capabilities drop sharply. QAH distills from the original model, a frozen teacher whose logits are precomputed offline, rather than from the recovered checkpoint. Source: paper Figure 1.

We applied QAH to a GPT-OSS 120B model, compressed to 60B parameters and recovered in bfloat16, then re-quantized to MXFP4 under QAH. The natural comparison is against that same 60B model's bfloat16 checkpoint, the best full-precision version of this architecture that exists. The QAH model wins on 7 of the 9 benchmarks.

The two benchmarks where QAH trails, MMLU-Pro and SciCode, lose by less than a point and a half. Everywhere else the 4-bit model is ahead of its own 16-bit source, and the largest gains land on exactly the capabilities compression usually damages most: long-context reasoning (+7.4 on AA-LCR) and math (+5.6 on AIME 2025).

The comparison against the original 120B teacher is just as telling. Despite running at half the teacher's parameter count and roughly a quarter of its weight memory, the QAH model surpasses the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench (66.5 vs. 66.0) and comes within 1.6 points on GPQA Diamond (67.4 vs. 69.0). The largest remaining gap against the teacher is on AA-LCR, an extreme long-context benchmark where the capacity lost to compression is intrinsically the hardest to recover.

The 4-bit QAH model matches or beats its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks, and beats the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench. Source: paper Figure 2.

To isolate the effect of the loss function from everything else, we also compared QAH directly against QAT under matched conditions, quantizing a GPT-OSS 9B model to MXFP4 and tracking average performance across MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA Diamond as training progresses.

Both methods reach a similar peak, 54.9 for QAH against 54.6 for QAT, so on best-case accuracy they are effectively tied. The difference is in how they get there and what happens afterwards. QAH reaches its peak in about 100 steps, roughly 7 times faster than QAT's 700, and then stays within about two points of that peak for the rest of training. QAT collapses sharply once past its peak, shedding nearly 19 points by step 1,200.

The practical consequence is a real deployment risk difference. A QAT checkpoint needs careful early stopping against a held-out signal to avoid shipping a model that has already started to degrade, whereas a sufficiently trained QAH checkpoint can be served safely because it simply does not drift. This is consistent with the mechanism: KL distillation against a frozen teacher gives the student no incentive to move once it matches the teacher, while a cross-entropy objective keeps pushing on hard labels and eventually erodes capabilities the model inherited from the original.

QAH peaks at 54.9 in roughly 100 steps and holds; QAT reaches 54.6 only around step 700, then loses nearly 19 points by step 1,200. Source: paper Figure 3.

The accuracy story comes paired with the efficiency story that motivated compression in the first place. At 4-bit precision the QAH model uses roughly 4 times less weight memory than the bfloat16 student, and at half the parameter count of the 120B teacher it roughly halves compute per token, which is what lets it run on substantially smaller hardware. For model families that ship in bfloat16 rather than 4-bit, the combined parameter and precision reduction would be closer to 8 times less compute per token.

The takeaway is that a compressed, 4-bit model does not have to be a lower-accuracy version of its full-precision counterpart. With this healing recipe it can be smaller, cheaper to serve, and more accurate at the same time, and it reaches that point in a fraction of the training a QAT recipe would need. Quantization stops being a tax you pay for efficiency and becomes an extra opportunity to teach the model.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making large models smaller and cheaper to run without giving up the capabilities that make them useful. It sits alongside our companion work on efficient distillation, which supplies the long-context training machinery QAH depends on.

Want the full technical details, including the healing pipeline, the chunked KL implementation for long-context healing, and the distributed-training findings? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying compression and healing to your own models.

The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as rbtv77 gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

This is a really fascinating take on model compression 🤯🔥. The idea that a 4-bit model can actually outperform the full-precision version turns the usual assumption about quantization completely upside down.... Instead of simply accepting the accuracy loss that comes with compression, QAH seems to show how targeted recovery can bring back—and even improve—important capabilities like reasoning, math, and coding. 🧠⚡

What really caught my attention is the result with the compressed GPT-OSS 120B → 60B model.... Getting a smaller MXFP4 model to beat its own bfloat16 checkpoint on 7 of 9 benchmarks is pretty impressive. 📊🚀 It makes the whole compress-then-heal pipeline feel much more practical for real-world deployment, especially when memory usage and inference costs matter.

I also like the broader implication here.... Quantization doesn't necessarily have to mean sacrificing model quality if the recovery process is designed with the quantized model in mind. 💡🔧 A smaller model that costs less to operate while still delivering stronger benchmark performance could be a huge advantage for teams trying to deploy capable LLMs efficiently.

Definitely an interesting direction for efficient AI deployment.... Turning a heavily compressed 4-bit model into something that can outperform its larger full-precision counterpart is the kind of result that makes you rethink what "compression" actually means. 👏🔥 Really curious to see how far Quantization-Aware Healing can go across other architectures and workloads.... 🚀🧠

Hi there! From how I'm reading this, I think you might have missed a method error in your experiment that invalidates your headline.

The headline comparison looks like it has no control. The bf16 60B got one round of distillation and the MXFP4 60B got that round plus a second round from a better teacher. The obvious missing comparison is to give the bf16 60B the identical second distillation pass in bf16, same data, same steps, same teacher. Without that comparison you cannot separate "QAH is a good recipe" from "we trained one checkpoint longer against a teacher than the other."

Results table labels the teacher "120B teacher (MXFP4)", which is right since gpt-oss-120b ships with MXFP4 MoE weights natively. But the approach section says the teacher is full-size and full-precision, and the title claims the student beats its full-precision original. Those contradict.

Unless I'm wrong, I'd retract this and consdier republishing when you can show the significant difference on the comparable arms without extending one further than the other with more compute.

You're right that the headline table compares checkpoints with unequal training. The 60B bf16 checkpoint got one distillation pass (the recovery); the 60B MXFP4 checkpoint got that pass plus a second one against the 120B teacher. We describe that second pass in the approach section, but we should have been explicit that the table therefore doesn't, on its own, separate "distilling under quantization" from "distilling for longer." We'll add that caveat to the text.

A bit of context on what the paper is: it's an applied case study, not a theoretical claim. The question we set out to answer is the one a deployment team faces: Given a compressed model that has to ship in 4 bits, what's the best way to run the quantization step? The result we stand behind is narrow and reproducible: the shipped 4-bit checkpoint scores above the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from, rather than below it, which is the usual outcome of direct post-training quantization. What we shouldn't have leaned into is the stronger causal reading, that quantization itself is "free training", and you're right that the current table doesn't isolate that.

The comparison that would settle it is the one you describe: the bf16 60B given the identical second pass. same data, steps, teacher and, separately, that continued bf16 checkpoint post-training-quantized to MXFP4. The second is really the decision anyone deploying faces: heal under quantization, or quantize afterwards. If we extend this for a revised version, those are the arms we'd add; either way we're flagging them as a limitation of the current version rather than claiming the table resolves the question.

We don't think retraction is the right call. The reported numbers are real and reproducible, and the practical result stands. But we agree the causal framing needs that control, and we'd rather correct it in the open than argue it. Appreciate the push.

#9754. Optimizing Rustc's next trait solver

The next rust trait solver, a large subsystem of the rust compiler that we've been trying to replace, will finally land in rust 1.102.0. In the last stages, before stabilizing it, its performance was a major blocker. But what is "a trait solver"? And why is its performance a problem? My goal for this blog post is to answer those questions in a way where you don't need any prior knowledge. I think discussions of the trait solver can quickly become quite involved, and daunting. So today, we'll start from the very basics!

This is a writeup of my eurorust 2026 talk of the same name, that I gave on October 15, 2026.

And if you'd rather watch than read this talk, you can do so here on youtube:

The new solver is the codebase I work on daily, and I've done so for about a year full-time. I'm not the main person driving its stabilization though, that would be lcnr , who's worked on it for far longer than I've been around in the Rust project. My main focus has been optimizing the new solver's performance.

Many people have worked avery hard, for years, to make the new solver a reality. You can find some of them here, and here.

My work here is only possible because of Hexcat and RustNL paying me and others to work on rust compiler development. Consider whether you or your company could sponsor Hexcat or the RustNL maintainer team.

On the 15th of May, 2015, Rust reached a major milestone. The very first stable version of rust was released. Version 1.0.0. Just 72 days later, on the 24th of July, work started on a new trait solver. Or well, that's when the Chalk project got its first commit. It seems the initial goal was to formalize the trait system so we could prove its correctness. One reason that didn't work well is because the trait system wasn't very correct at all.

Chalk is, according to its github description, "An implementation and definition of the Rust trait system using a PROLOG-like logic solver". The fact that it's "PROLOG-like" we'll come back to in a few paragraphs, it's quite interesting! However, Chalk isn't around anymore. Its README.md says it has been "sunset in favor of the newer next-generation trait solver". In October 2022, this project was officially started to turn the lessons learned from Chalk, into an actual new subsystem of the rust compiler, that, once finished, could replace the code of the old trait solver.

The goal of the new trait solver is to make sure we wouldn't have as many correctness bugs in the trait system. We now call this project "project zero", referring to the number of soundness bugs we'd ideally like to have in our type system. There have been several very long standing bugs in Rust's (old) trait solver. Like this one, that has been open since May 28, 2015 (just 13 days after Rust 1.0!). It abuses something called "implied bounds" to convince the Rust compiler to turn a short lifetime 'a into a 'static lifetime, allowing you to use a reference after its already freed. Some of these bugs were fundamentally impossible to fix with the way the old trait solver worked.

Note: Chalk and the new trait solver aren't the same thing. Chalk came first, and learned a lot of lessons incorporated in the new solver.

But what is a trait system? And how does a trait solver solve it?

The first place to look for documentation about the Rust compiler is the "rustc dev guide". It says "The goal of the trait system is to check whether a given trait bound is satisfied. Most notably when typechecking the body of - potentially generic - functions.". But I promised I'd start at absolute zero, so what's a trait?

Some types act in similar ways. They share certain properties. For example, a lot of different types can be cloned, or copared for equality. To codify these properties, we can use traits. In other words, a trait is a property of a type.

Notably, you can associate behaviors with these properties. The standard library's definition of Clone also includes two methods that can be called to perform this cloning operation.

To check whether the code you wrote is correct, the Rust compiler sometimes has to check that these properties hold. If you're trying to clone a value, the compiler has to check whether that value can be cloned.

Prolog is a cool programming language that works and looks very differently to what you may be used to. However, it is just as powerful (i.e. turing complete) as any other. The way it works has strong parallels to our trait system, let me show you. Here's an example:

A Prolog program consists of a set of statements, called "facts", as well as relationships between facts. In the above program, there are two facts: u64 has the property Copy, String has the property Clone, And there's also a relationship between these two properties. If some variable x has the Copy property, it also has the Clone property.

Finally, we can ask the prolog program some questions. For example, Does the type u64 have the Clone property? To answer that question, the runtime of a prolog program has to analyze all the known facts and relations. In this program we haven't said that u64 has the Clone property. However, we have said that it has the Copy property. And by using the relationship between Copy and Clone, the solver can derive that both questions (starting with ?-) are true!

The reason Chalk was using a "prolog-like" solver, is because as you can see, the trait system is extremely similar to a logic solver. Both "facts" and "relations" can be written using impl blocks. In fact, I can write the above program as a Rust program:

Neither the new solver or the old solver state as plainly as chalk does that they're using a "prolog-like solver". However, given the similarities, both the old solver and the new solver really aren't so different from how you'd implement a prolog runtime.

Trait solving is not the same as type inference. This is a common misconception. Inside the Rust compiler, the two are completely different subsystems. Type inference is the process of replacing blanks with types. Throughout this text I'll refer to some the following example code (with slight variations):

We use type inference to determine that the type of the variable a is an integer. The same for b.

Having said that, sometimes during type inference we do have to ask things about traits, and will call into the trait solver. Furthermore, the trait solver sometimes "unifies type variables", which means that while Rust makes a query about traits, we might make some progress on figuring out what the types of some variables are.

In the example code, one place where the trait solver comes into effect is when we call weird_add. On the function there's a where bound. A where bound is a requirement that the Rust compiler must check before allowing a call to that function. In this case, Rust has to make sure that i32 (a type we found through type inference) implements the Add trait. To do that, the solver can use one of a couple of strategies, and we'll look at each. In this case, we'll be looking for an impl block that mentions the i32 type, and we'll find one of those in the standard library!

Once the trait solver finds this impl block, it acts as an answer to the question "does i32 implement Add?". We somtimes refer to this answer as a a proof that the statement holds.

The example code contains several more calls to the trait solver. One you may not have thought about is that all local variables in Rust have to implement the Sized trait to be allowed on the stack. The Sized trait codifies that the compiler knows how many bytes of memory the value takes up, so it can be allocated on the stack. So, there will also be a query to the trait solver asking "does i32 implement Sized?".

The proof for this statement doesn't come from an impl block though. I did say that the compiler has several stratagies to derive proofs. In this case, the fact that some primitive types implement Sized is built-in to the compiler. i32 is inherently Sized, and there is no impl block anywhere that says so.

Answering Sized queries in general turns out to be quite hard because of the shear volume at which it occurs. To compile rust's standard library, we'll ask "does type implement Sized?" about 800 000 times! Additionally, answering it isn't always this simple. Let's take a slightly more involved example:

To prove Kitten: Sized, a recursive process takes place. Both fields have to implement Sized too. So in the process of answering this question, the trait solver will produce more questions to be answered. Kitten: Sized leads to String: Sized & f64: Sized. f64 luckily is trivial again, and built into the compiler. String isn't though, and we go one more layer deeper to Vec: Sized, etcetera.

In Rust, generic functions can be type checked standalone. The example using weird_add doesn't need a main function to be checked, and may emit its own type errors.

This is where the trait solver actually does the most work. For example, to type check weird_add, we have to prove that a + b is valid. a + b desugars to a.add(b), and when finding the method add the trait solver gets invoked, since the add method comes from the Add trait.

Previously, proof candidates came either from impl blocks or they were built into the compiler. Not here though! A new proof strategy is used here instead. When calling weird_add we saw that a where bound acts as a requirement that has to be checked before calling, but that means that inside weird_add we can assume that where bound holds and thus it acts as a proof strategy. Concretely, we know a has the type T, and to answer the question "does T implement Add" we find a where bound that says so.

Add isn't the only trait bound that has to be proven inside weird_add. This is another place where we have to prove that T: Sized. Again we have to look for candidates, and there's no built in one for generic types T, nor is there an impl block, nor a where bound that mentions Sized. So how does that work? Well, it turns out the where bound is implicit. T: Add really means T: Add + Sized, and so proving Sized works the same as proving Add.

On lobsters I got asked about whether the Add bound is required to add the Sized bound. The T: Sized implicit bound gets added for any generic. Even if there was not already an Add bound, T would still be Sized. Currently, you can opt out of that implicit bound using T: ?Sized (or in the example, T: Add + ?Sized). In the future we may change the syntax for that to T: MetaSized. Look for the keyword "Sized Hierarchy" if you want to learn more. This document should also give you a primer.

Finally, this code will actually give a type error, because there's one more trait to prove. Because b gets mentioned twice, we have to clone or copy values of type T. The function signature really should have been:

To summarize, trait solving is the process of answering questions about relations between types and traits. These questions are submitted to the trait solver, and the trait solver looks for candidates in the form of:

When it finds one of these, we say we've found a proof, and if we cannot find one, a type error is emitted.

Sofar, all trait solving came down to finding a single candidate, but that's not always how it works. Let's look at the definition of the From and the Into traits:

If the trait solver gets a question like u32: Into (does u32 implement the Into trait), it will find the impl block above. However, the impl block is generic, and has a where bound that says "T implements Into U IF U implements From T". Luckily there's another impl block that gives that implementation and so the initial statement can be proven.

What this all means, is that while answering a question, the trait solver emits more questions. These subquestions get added to an internal queue in the trait solver, and this queue of questions will be proven one after the other. Like this, some questions can turn into several subquestions, which can even have their own subquestions again.

Also, in the example from above, the second question actually has two proofs! There are two impl blocks that apply, since there's also this blanket implementation for identity conversion:

Some preference takes place here. Since this is a blanket implementation, the other more specific one takes precedence. We can think about the trait solving about answering a tree of candidates that may apply. In this case, the single candidate for u32: Into turns into two, u64: From and T: From.

Something we'll not cover today, but this tree of candidates in reality is not a tree, it can have cycles! This has been the cause of both many bugs, and many rust compiler developers' nightmares.

The trait solver doesn't just deal with traits. An important thing it has to also consider is the associated types of traits. Let's look at the Add trait:

An implementation of the Add trait can decide what the Output type will be equal to. Remember the definition of Add for integers?

It says that when you add two i32s, we get back an i32. The reason the trait solver cares about associated types is that sometimes answering questions creates subquestions that mention associated types.

Because we wrote Output = T, the trait solver has to check that the candidate impl block has an Output type that's equal to T. We could've also written a more general function signature to something like:

Or really to make it works you have to go one step further (click to expand).

Hold on! impl blocks can define inputs they act on, like impl Foo for i32 applies when the input is i32. It can make these inputs variables, like impl Foo for T. And impl blocks can also define outputs thrugh associated types.

What we've done here, is make impl blocks powerful enough to act as functions, with inputs and outputs. And Alonzo Church proved that a language with only pure functions is in fact turing complete.

This is why Prolog is a fully-fledged turing complete programming language, and so is Rust's type system. People have defined numbers completely in Rust's type system in a crate called typenum, and have gone even further by implementing a chess engine inside the type system.

Trait solving ends up being a subsystem that the compiler spends quite a large portion of its time in. In general, there are two reasons for that:

This ends up replacing the trait solver more complicated than you might think. People have already written many programs using the old solver, and because the new solver internally makes different assumptions (sometimes in the name of soundness, remember the old solver has many bugs), we end up having programs that take both longer and shorter to compile. Sometimes with a polynomial factor, sometimes even with an exponential factor.

For example, the crate unic-ucd contains code along the lines of:

It lists a whole bunch of unicode characters, and each constant inside these slices are themselves string literals. That means each of them has an associated lifetime variable, that at some point gets inferred to 'static since we're assigning to a const. Now the new trait solver, in some cases where the old solver did not, reasons about lifetimes.

Now sometimes, the rust compiler attempts see if two types are equal. This process may have side effects, in that it may make some progress towards inferring other types in the program. Because these side effects are sometimes undesireable, we have a system to "attempt" to unify types, and then roll back the results. To be able to do rollbacks we sometimes keep a trace of all operations we perform, so we can run them in reverse to get back to where we started. However, sometimes this tracking is more expensive than simply making a copy of the state and putting that copy back.

In this case, during borrow checking, we call into the the trait solver and end up unifying two "lifetime variables", which we roll back. This specific rollback involves a copy, though there was a shortcut. We keep track of a single boolean: "was any lifetime variable modified". If none were, the rollback can be skipped. The old solver wouldn't do such unifications, so the rollback could always be skipped, while in the new solver we couldn't do so.

Often, there are very few lifetime variables in scope, so doing a rollback isn't so bad. However, the example above lists every unicode character in existence, so the list is rather long. And for every item in the list, we'd do such a rollback, that copied all lifetime variables (for which there is one per element in the list). So N undos copying a list of N lifetime variables, that's a quadratic factor! So this crate would compile just fine with the old solver, and be 200 times slower with the new solver. Oops!

There are two important strategies we use to make the trait solver faster. First of all, there's caching, and a lot of it. For example, in the following example we prove that i32: Sized three times:

We'd like to make it so we only need to figure out whether a specific type is Sized once, and so we cache the result.

The second optimization we use a lot is not caching funnily enough. Accessing the cache can be rather expensive (we'll get to why). So in this case, since i32 is trivially Sized, we can answer the question faster by never looking in the cache. For more complicated types this is not true.

A naive cache would be a mapping from questions asked to the trait solver, to answers (errors or proofs). So, something like HashMap, but this wouldn't perform so well. Let's look at this example:

Here we've renamed the variables T and U between foo and bar. We'll prove two question, that T: Into and later U: Into. Because of the renamings these two proofs are the same, but the questions are technically different. If we don't do something about variable renaming, we'd have cache misses all the time.

Another issue is that this cache wouldn't even work. By now, we've learned that candidates for proofs can come from three sources:

The first two play nicely, because the same impl blocks and compiler built-ins are around for all questions submitted to the trait solver. Howver, where bounds are different for every function, and thus a proof that a type implements a trait inside of one function, may not be reusable inside another function.

In the example above, we prove that T: Into twice. Inside foo that's ok, but not inside of bar. So if we naively cached that T: Into we wouldn't notice that bar is incorrect.

We call the set of bounds that are in-scope during trait solving the ParamEnv (parameter environment), and so the cache would really have to look like HashMap<(ParamEnv, Question), Answer>. Since for every function, the ParamEnv is different, we'd have even more cache misses.

To improve our chances of a cache hit, we perform a process called "Canonicalization". During canonicalization, we do two things. First we'll rename all variables with numbers. So, T: Into will become ?0: Into (variable 0 implements Into variable 1). Since this process is consistent, another renamed input like U: Into also gets this numbering and is compatible.

In addition, we'll try very hard to figure out which where bounds in the ParamEnv actually matter. If there are bounds that won't affect the result of the query, we can avoid putting them in the cache key, making cache hits more likely.

So, in the rust compiler, the cache really looks more like a HashMap<(Paramenv, CanonicalQuestion), CanonicalAnswer> Note that the answer of every query now has to be de-canonicalized. We call this "instantiation". When we turn T: Into into ?0: Into, and cache its result, and we later look for U: Into, we have to turn the answer (that mentions variables 0 and 1) into U and T respectively. In other words, by canonicalizing we make cache hits much more likely, but the process isn't free. Hence not caching is sometimes worth it for simple questions.

Now is this worth it? Below I've plotted the hit rate of the new solver's cache for various popular crates, and one internal rust compiler benchmark.

As you can see, we can often avoid almost 80% of all trait solving by caching. The last two bars are for a crate called wg-grammar. It is a crate that used to be particularly slow with the new trait solver. Part of my job this year used to be specifically optimizing it.

The problem was that there's one more property that has to be part of the cache key: which opaque types are in scope. An opaque type is a type you write as a "return position impl trait". For example:

foo returns impl IntoIterator. By doing so, callers of this function don't get to know what specific type is returned. Only that they can iterate over whatever they get back. Inside of this function foo, the trait solver will infer which specific type gets returned (a Vec), but in other functions calling foo, this information is not available. So, this is another piece of information that may affect answers from function to function, just like the ParamEnv.

So, the real cache has one more input: HashMap<(ParamEnv, OpaqueTypes, CanonicalQuestion), CanonicalAnswer>. What that really means is that the following two functions both submit the question i32: Clone to the trait solver, but cannot reuse the cache entry:

This ends up mattering a lot in async code, or code like parser-generators that tend to return -> impl Parser from functions. That's unfortunate, because the fact that opaque types are different ends up almost never affecting the outcome of a question. Sure, we can come up with examples where it does, but in practice it almost never does.

So, the fix here is to remove opaque types from the cache key to the cached value like so: HashMap<(ParamEnv, CanonicalQuestion), (CanonicalAnswer, OpaqueTypeState)>. Then, every time we answer a question that may be different because of opaque types, we record in the opaque type state under what condition it may affect the answer, and continue assuming the answer is unaffected (this is often the case). Then, when we get a cached answer in a specific environment, we look at the opaque type state, to see whether the answer might be affected by current context. It almost never is, but if it ends up mattering, we retry the question but now no longer assuming opaque types don't matter.

This sometimes makes performance worse (we sometimes do double work), but since its so rare, we get an improvement over all by having more cache hits. In the graph from above, there are two bars for wg-grammar. One where the hit rate is 73% and one where the hit rate is 79%. This 6% difference translates to some the wg-grammar crate first taking 28 seconds to compile, and afterwards only 14 seconds. That's 2x faster!

(click to expand for me going into a little more detail about this)

Technically even when we use opaque type tracking, the list of opaques is still part of the key. We just set it to be an empty list. That means that in the rerun, we un-empty it and we get a different cache key. Now because we keep the cache entry with the empty list around too, when a new query comes along it will also empty the list, find a cache hit that matches this empty list but with tracking information (so it's not redoing work getting that tracking). Then, if it decides it needs to rerun, it adds back the list of opaques and could totally get a cache hit again if we've tried with those exact opaques before.

Of note is also that sometimes we run multiple dependent queries without their opaques like this. We can only un-empty the list once we get back up to the root at the point where we emptied the list to see if they may be unnecessary. To make sure we don't spend too much time running giant query trees we have a bailing mechanism built in to the tracking. Once a query and it's dependencies try to access opaques more than 3 times (or when they do so in very specific ways) we assume that it's unlikely for opaques not to influence the outcome of the query in any way, and we bail out of the "erased" attempts (recording in each dependent result that it's likely a rerun is necessary) and rerun without every knowing the original (erased) result, since it's unlikely to be correct. Future queries will see that this happened in the tracking information, and never attempt to erase opaque types. They know that the attempt is likely wasted.

Now there's an even more subtle thing going on. Sometimes assuming that opaques are empty (in a specific path related to coroutines) leads to query cycles. So, in that case we are forced to do this bailing and to rerun with opaque types even if the answer would've maybe been correct with the erased environment, because the compiler would crash if it encountered the cycle and we want to avoid those at all costs. In this case we may end up rerunning with opaque types, get to the exact same point, and continue to return the exact same result as we would have when we erased the environment previously. This is sadly unavoidable.

This, and more optimizations meant that wg-grammar used to take almost 200 Billion cpu cycles to compile, and now only about 7 Billion.

Now this is my second blog post about trait solver optimization. The other one is a little more technical, and goes into all the different things we did over the past year to bring the new trait solver towards stabilization. Go read it next if you're interested, and thank you for reading! If you're still interested in learning more about this, I'm happy to answer any questions if you reach out.

Also, hell yea! you made it to the end. Here's my cat.

#9753. In Security, Words Matter as Much as Tools — Maybe More

From talking cloud security to using AI, cyber leaders are finding that clear, disciplined communication is now a front-line defense capability across the enterprise.

The best tool cyber teams can wield to defend their organizations has nothing to do with tech; it's how they talk. Whether the audience is the C-suite, the development team, or the sheepish user who just fell for a phish, communications savvy is increasingly mission-critical.

During a Dark Reading Virtual Event panel I recently put together to talk tech, tools, integration, and frameworks, called "Key Tools & Technologies for Locking Down Your Cloud," SANS instructor Ahmed AbuGharbia urged cybersecurity teams to "learn the language of the cloud" to build credibility with IT, and to do the same for developers. We discussed technology and products, too, but I was surprised at the amount of time that was spent on stressing the importance of communication and language when it comes to having effective conversations with vendors, executives, and users.

My other panelist, Theresa Lanowitz, a principal analyst at Omdia, detailed the distinction between security "of" the cloud and security "in" the cloud, noting that under existing shared responsibility models, cloud service providers assume responsibility "of" the cloud itself, rather than what organizations decide to put "in" the cloud.

Related:Cyber Insurers See New Divide: AI Defense 'Haves' & 'Have Nots'

This wasn't the first time I had noticed a shift in the way security practitioners focus on a commitment to using effective language.

A couple of weeks ago I sat in several sessions at the ISC2 Strategic Conference in Denver that spent a remarkable amount of time on strategies for clearly communicating risk and documenting those exchanges in much the same way as they would any other log, piece of evidence, or asset. In the past, these conversations would have been more focused on translating tech talk into corporate speak. CISOs have worked for a long time on how to talk to leadership about risk and budget; it's been an ongoing conversation for several years. However, emphasis on how cyber teams can learn to ask the right questions not just of leadership, but pertinent people both inside and outside the business, feels like a fresh effort. Using precise language and presenting strategic (not just technical and tactical) concepts effectively is no longer being discussed as a nice thing for security pros to be able to do, but critical to fundamental enterprise defense.

For example, CISO and expert Laura Vaughn has cleverly broken down threat modeling into 4 Simple Questions on a White Board. Her strategy distills years of experience and technical expertise into plain language anyone can understand, like, "What [cyber incident] would hurt most on Monday morning?" That honed language helps get teams to the heart of the threats, and helps them understand the work that needs to happen next. That all saves time and money, and eliminates the scariest risks first. Other deceptively simple questions she suggests asking include, "Who hacks organizations like ours and how?" And, "What is the cheapest control?" Smart comms informs and focuses the technical work.

Related:How Southeastern University Got a Handle on Its Data

Likewise, technologist and attorney Daniel B. Garrie, CEO of Law and Forensics, presents language as a frontline defense, and coaches CISOs and cyber leaders on the finer points of contract negotiations. He advocates rigorous documentation of communications on risk and defense decisions, so those decisions would be defensible later, and so that transparency can help drive cybersecurity across the organization.

The introduction of AI is also requiring cybersecurity teams to pick their words carefully. AI has put a language interface between the user and compute operations that benefits those who can ask the best questions. Likewise, experts across the cyber sector urge caution around using humanizing language to describe AI agents or attribute human motivation to their actions.

Related:US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise

Being an expert communicator is no longer a skill that's nice to have in cybersecurity; it's fundamental to enterprise defense. Be precise in the words you choose, and meet your audiences where they are. You might be surprised to find it's becoming the most powerful tool you or your organization could ever deploy against the next threat.

[Virtual Event] Cybersecurity Outlook 2027

Just in time for the new year, Cybersecurity Outlook 2027 will look ahead at some of the newest threats posed by cybercriminals and nation-states, as well as evolving technologies that may help mitigate those threats as AI proliferates. You'll hear from some of the cybersecurity industry's leading analysts and experts, as well as researchers who have been examining the next wave of cyber threats, AI-driven technologies and other cybersecurity tools to help organizations defend their multi-cloud and hybrid environments.

Award-winning journalist and senior editor at Dark Reading reporting across diverse media platforms, including podcasts and video. Becky is passionate about delivering insightful, high-quality information and storytelling that informs and engages the cybersecurity community. Her specific focus is on the intersection of cybersecurity and public policy and its impact on the enterprise.

As the host and producer of the recently Azbee-recognized Dark Reading Confidential podcast, she presents compelling conversations with industry leaders, exploring the latest trends and challenges in cybersecurity. Becky is also the moderator Dark Reading's popular editorial webinars, and oversees Dark Reading's Commentary section, curating expert perspectives intended to drive meaningful dialogue. Additionally, she is the host of Dark Reading's Black Hat News Desk, delivering timely and in-depth coverage right from the heart of one of the industry's most important events.

Beyond editorial responsibilities, Becky is a regular writer and reporter for Dark Reading, contributing articles that delve into the evolving cybersecurity landscape.

InfoQ Homepage News Vercel Launched Experimental Board to Coordinate Tasks Across Humans and Coding Agents

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read

Vercel has launched Vercel Board, an experimental, headless message board where people and coding agents coordinate tasks across tools and harnesses. Vercel says Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, eve, fx, Mastra, and LangChain can work on the same board as if they were a single harness.

Each Vercel team gets a default board, named General, organized into channels and threads. Developers and agents read and write through the `vercel board` CLI or the `@vercel/board` JavaScript SDK. A skill, installed with npx skills add vercel/board --skill board, teaches coding agents the CLI. Agents name themselves with --as or BOARD_PROFILE, but still act with the operator's or project's credentials.

A task is a thread whose state the board keeps. A worker claims a ready task, posts updates, and completes or fails it. A claim is a lease of up to five minutes and must be renewed; if it expires, the task returns to the queue. When two workers claim the same task, one succeeds and the other fails with task_claimed. Tasks can declare dependencies, so a review waits until its fix completes while independent work proceeds in parallel. Watchers on a Vercel deployment can run when a reply is posted or a label changes, waking the deployment so no process has to stay running.

Sync, configured in the SDK and delivered through Vercel Connect, can attach a board channel to Slack, GitHub, or Linear. Slack and Linear sync both ways; GitHub imports pull requests and issues and does not write back unless the project sends those messages. Grants control who can read, post, and manage each channel. For an agent in a Vercel Sandbox, sandboxPolicy() can grant limited board access without putting a credential inside the sandbox. Vercel says it rebuilt v0's software factory on Board, and that the factory now merges over 50% of its pull requests.

Official documentation warns that Board grants do not apply on Slack, GitHub, or Linear, so a private Slack channel synced into an open board channel is readable by the whole Vercel team.

Austin King (@MadeWithOzten) replied to Vercel's announcement asking to

Do this self-hosted and open source - Rust, Yjs Sync,

then wrote that he had bought openboard.lol

For a self-hosted open source Vercel board like thing.

Aaron Delz (@AaronDelz) said he already kept a shared checklist with his agent, and liked that a Board task can be completed with the pull request attached:

Same rule my agents run on: no saying 'done' without the evidence.

Similar coordination shows up elsewhere. OpenCrawl is an open source, self-hostable board that also records agent sessions. GitHub Agent HQ can assign issues and pull requests to Copilot, Claude, or Codex. Linear's cloud coding agent turns scoped issues into draft pull requests with Claude Code or Codex. Claude Code agent teams coordinate multiple Claude Code sessions around a shared task list, and the Agent2Agent protocol standardizes delegation between agents rather than hosting a board.

Board remains experimental infrastructure on a Vercel team. Setup steps and the CLI and SDK references are in Vercel's Board documentation

#9751. Granite 4.2 LLMs: How They're Built

A technical walkthrough of how we built the Granite 4.2 reasoning model family.

TL;DR: Granite 4.2 is our first family of dense, decoder-only reasoning LLMs, released in three sizes: 3B, 8B, and 30B. These models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were pre-trained from scratch on roughly 15T tokens with a five-phase strategy that extends the context window to 512K tokens, supervised fine-tuned on chain-of-thought, reasoning, and agentic-trajectory data, then post-trained with a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline. That pipeline includes agentic RL, where the 8B and 30B models learn to act with tools inside real sandboxed environments. Every model has a thinking / non-thinking switch, a low-effort thinking mode that spends a short reasoning budget on easy questions, and native tool calling. All Granite 4.2 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Granite 4.2 is the reasoning-focused release of the Granite language-model family. Earlier Granite releases were strong instruction-following assistants; Granite 4.2 adds explicit reasoning. Every model can produce a chain of thought before its answer and can run in thinking or non-thinking mode depending on how much deliberation a task needs. A low-effort mode falls between the two, spending a short reasoning budget on easy questions.

The three sizes (3B, 8B, and 30B) share the same architectural design and follow the same training pipeline (base model, SFT, then multi-stage RL), each at its own scale. All three are strong reasoners and instruction followers. The clearest capability split shows up in post-training. The 8B and 30B models additionally go through an agentic RL block that teaches them to operate as agents: calling tools, editing and running code, driving a terminal, and searching the web inside real environments. Every model supports native tool calling. Served through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (for example, with vLLM), it emits tool calls in the OpenAI function-calling format and plugs into agentic harnesses without extra glue. Granite 4.2 is also supported in SGLang, see the SGLang cookbook for a ready-to-serve recipe.

The rest of this post walks through the build: architecture, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, the multi-stage RL pipeline, and results.

Granite 4.2 models are built on a decoder-only dense transformer architecture with the following core components:

Granite 4.2 models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five-phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre-training, phases 3–4 perform mid-training with progressively higher-quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long-context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase uses a distinct data mixture and learning-rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web-scale data toward more curated, high-quality sources.

The pre-training recipe closely follows the previous generation; for a detailed treatment of the data blend, phase schedule, and long-context extension, see the Granite 4.1 blog.

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) turns the base model into a reliable instruction-following, reasoning, and tool-using assistant. The SFT data mixture combines agentic (31.6%) and non-agentic (68.4%) data, totaling approximately 7.2 million samples, or roughly 100B tokens, of which about 65B are trainable.

The agentic corpus covers a broad range of domains, including software engineering (SWE, 69%), tool calling (12.1%), terminal use (8.0%), math (3.5%), search (0.8%), and action (0.2%). These samples and trajectories are generated using a diverse set of agent scaffolds and harnesses, including OpenHands, OpenCode, Terminus-2, SWE-agent, OpenResearcher, MiniSWE, OpenSeeker, EnvScaler, Gemini CLI, Hermes, Codex, and Goose. The agentic data combines samples from both open-source datasets and our own synthetically generated RL environments, spanning a variety of agent–harness combinations.

The non-agentic corpus consists of several major categories: instruction following (18.8%), coding (18.8%), math (14.6%), multilingual (7.0%), science (5.4%), reasoning (3.0%), and safety (0.8%).

We apply multiple stages of quality control before a sample enters the final SFT mixture. First, data from different sources is normalized and reformatted into a consistent OpenAI Chat format, making the conversation structure and tool interactions uniform across datasets and scaffolds.

We then use GPT-OSS-120B and Gemma 4 as LLM-based judges to assess sample quality. Low-scoring samples are removed, as are samples containing hallucinated or fabricated information, invalid tool interactions, or tool calls to functions that are not defined in the corresponding tool list. Several targeted, dataset-specific heuristic rules are also applied where appropriate to further improve quality and remove known sources of noise.

Finally, we perform both local and global deduplication. Deduplication is based on SHA-256 hashes computed over the combination of the tools and messages fields, removing duplicate samples both within individual data sources and across the overall SFT mixture.

The complete corpus is first globally shuffled to reduce ordering effects and ensure that samples from different domains are well mixed during training. The shuffled corpus is then partitioned into equally sized .parquet shards, which are tokenized using the model's tokenizer and chat template and prepared for large-scale distributed training.

Before launching the final large-scale runs, we tune hyperparameters on representative configurations, sweeping learning-rate schedules, initial learning rates, and warm-up ratios to find settings that train stably across model sizes. The final training configuration is summarized below:

For the 30B model, we additionally perform a second phase of SFT focused specifically on agentic coding. In this phase, agentic, SWE, and coding data are upsampled to increase their effective contribution to the training distribution, while approximately 16% of the mixture is retained as replay data from the original SFT corpus.

The 30B model is then fine-tuned for roughly one additional epoch at a lower learning rate of 3.0e-6. This targeted second phase increases the model's exposure to agentic coding trajectories without discarding the capabilities acquired during the initial SFT phase.

After SFT, we apply a multi-stage, multi-environment reinforcement learning pipeline. Rather than a single RL pass, we run a chain of focused stages spanning many environments: math, code, science, instruction following, tool use, and structured output, then software engineering, terminal use, and web search. Each stage is an independent RL run that targets one capability and warm-starts from the previous stage's checkpoint.

Figure 1. The staged RL curriculum. Foundational RL (verifiable rewards + skill boosters) runs for all sizes; the agentic RL block (SWE → Terminal → Search) runs for 8B and 30B only. Every model finishes with RLHF. Each stage is a separate GRPO run that warm-starts from the previous checkpoint.

Every stage trains with asynchronous GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), so the generator and trainer halves of the loop never block on each other. A pool of generation workers keeps sampling responses and dropping the finished trajectories into a shared buffer; once the buffer holds a full step's worth, the trainer pulls that batch, takes an optimizer step, and streams the updated parameters back to the generator workers without pausing them. A refresh can land partway through a rollout, leaving a single trajectory stitched together from two adjacent policy versions. We allow this instead of paying to prevent it: the workers reuse their existing KV cache rather than rebuilding it after each refresh, and the one guardrail is a limit that keeps them from drifting more than a single update behind the trainer, which bounds how off-policy any sample can get. Whatever mismatch survives that limit is handled in the objective by truncated importance sampling, which clamps the train-versus-generation log-probability ratio to a fixed ceiling so a handful of stale tokens cannot dominate an update.

Advantages are group-relative with a leave-one-out baseline: each response is judged against the mean reward of the other samples drawn for the same prompt, which removes the need for a separate value network. To make this concrete, take RLVR, the first and longest-running stage: each step pairs 256 prompts with 16 sampled responses apiece for a 4,096-example batch, which the trainer consumes in a single optimizer step before the next rollout begins. Later stages keep this machinery unchanged and adjust only the per-stage shape, shown next.

The pipeline keeps a common backbone of hyperparameters across every stage, which makes the curriculum easier to run and compare. A handful of knobs are fixed everywhere:

What changes from stage to stage is the shape of each run: how many prompts and generations per step, how long the context is, whether the agent loop runs, and how hard we pull back toward the reference policy. The table below gives the exact settings for the 30B chain, stage by stage:

Parameters shown for the 30B model. Global batch size = prompts/step × generations/prompt (e.g. 256 × 16 = 4096 for RLVR). The 3B and 8B models use the same recipe and hyperparameters with fewer stages (see How the Three Sizes Differ); the stage list is what changes, not the knobs.

The KL schedule follows the reward type: explore freely where the reward is objective and verifiable (RLVR and SWE 2 run at KL 0), and stay close to the reference where the objective is preference, safety, or a narrow skill graft (RLHF and the code booster use KL 0.05). The rollout-turns column counts the environment interactions GRPO itself sees per rollout. In every case the model is trained on complete, real-environment trajectories.

Each stage is a separate RL run with a single objective and its own reward signal. When it finishes, its policy is exported to Hugging Face format and becomes the base model for the next stage, so the pipeline is a sequence of warm-starts:

The 8B and 30B models follow the full ladder. The 3B model takes a shortened path: foundational RL and alignment, without the agentic block.

A stage is defined mostly by how it is rewarded. Across the pipeline there are three reward types, and a single stage can use more than one:

Verifiable rewards are objective and hard to game, so the pipeline front-loads them. Judge- and preference-based rewards handle open-ended qualities that no checker can express. Agentic-outcome rewards are the sparsest: often a single bit at the end of a long tool-use trajectory.

RLVR is the foundational stage and the broadest data mix in the pipeline: a single blended dataset spanning many verifiable domains.

Each task type carries its own verifier, so the reward is grounded per example. RLVR runs for two rounds on 3B and 8B, and three on 30B. Each round is a fresh warm-started run on a re-weighted mix of public and internally curated RL data.

After RLVR, a few short booster stages sharpen specific capabilities that benefit from concentrated training focusing on the following domains:

Boosters are small, focused runs. A light KL penalty keeps the model close to its current behavior while nudging one skill.

In the agentic stages the model learns to act: call tools, observe results, and iterate inside a real environment, rewarded on whether the task was actually solved. These stages share the same shape: multi-turn tool use, real (not simulated) environments, sparse outcome rewards, and GRPO, warm-started from the coding-boosted checkpoint. They run in order: SWE → Terminal → Search.

Figure 2. The three agentic-RL environments. Each pairs a real harness with a real environment and a sparse, outcome-based reward. The 3B model runs none of these.

The final stage of every model is RLHF for human preference and safety. It optimizes against a generative reward model (GenRM) for preference, plus a safety reward covering jailbreak resistance and appropriate refusals. This stage uses the highest KL penalty in the pipeline, aligning tone and safety without eroding the capabilities the earlier stages built. In addition to human preference and safety alignment, this stage also applies a reasoning-length penalty to discourage overly verbose reasoning behavior acquired during earlier stages.

Same method and infrastructure; the difference is how far up the ladder each model goes.

3B is a strong foundational-RL model; 8B and 30B add the agentic-RL block on top, learning to act with tools in real environments.

Reinforcement learning at this scale needs infrastructure that can drive a training loop and a fleet of live environments at the same time. This matters most in the agentic stages, where every training example is a multi-turn rollout that edits code, runs commands, or browses the web. Granite 4.2's RL runs on two open components: NeMo-RL on the training side and NeMo-Gym on the rollout side.

Figure 3. The RL system. NeMo-RL drives the GRPO loop (Megatron-Core training backend, vLLM generation, and Megatron-Bridge for HF⇄Megatron weight conversion). NeMo-Gym orchestrates rollouts and hosts the tools, sandboxes, and reward/verifier calls as pluggable Resources.

That uniformity is what makes the staged curriculum above practical: a booster's rule-based checker and a full SWE sandbox present the same interface to GRPO.

This split is also what makes the asynchronous training loop described above physically possible: generation and policy updates live on separate GPU pools, so the expensive generation fleet — including the live agentic environments — stays busy instead of idling through optimizer steps.

Granite 4.2 was evaluated across agentic coding, general agentic and tool use, reasoning, chat and instruction following, and long context. The full benchmark table is below, followed by charts that break out the headline results by model size.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

The charts below break these results out by capability area.

Figure 4. Reasoning (pass@1). Scores rise consistently with model size across math (AIME25, HMMT), science (GPQA), and code reasoning (LiveCodeBench, SciCode).

Figure 5. Agentic coding resolve rates. The agentic-RL block is trained only for 8B and 30B; the 30B model leads across SWE-Bench variants and Terminal-Bench.

Figure 6. General agentic and tool-use benchmarks, reported for all three sizes.

We also released four quantized variants of the Granite 4.2 models for inference with vLLM. The models are converted to FP8, NVFP4, and MXFP4 using LLM Compressor, and to the GGUF format using the llama.cpp framework for reduced-memory deployment.

The FP8 version is quantized with dynamic per-channel weights and per-token activations. No calibration is used.

The NVFP4 and MXFP4 versions are quantized using GPTQ calibrated on 2K samples drawn from the SFT dataset. Max context length is 2K during calibration.

Conversion of the Granite 4.2 models to GGUF is done with the canonical llama.cpp tool as described in https://github.com/IBM/gguf#gguf-conversion--quantization.

We trained the Granite 4.2 language models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted by CoreWeave, featuring:

This infrastructure delivers the high-bandwidth, low-latency communication required for efficient large-scale distributed training.

The training software stack is packaged into .sqsh container images, each giving a run a reproducible, portable environment with its SBSA-compatible CUDA targets, Linux aarch64 Python wheels, and GPU-specific binaries pinned. The large-scale SFT runs build on an NGC PyTorch base image (Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.8, Python 3.12); the RL stack runs in its own NeMo-RL container.

Granite models support tool calling with integrated reasoning: the model reasons about which tool to call and why before calling it. Tools are defined with the OpenAI function definition schema.

Granite models can serve as the backbone for agentic coding tools. Because they support reasoning and tool calling through the OpenAI-compatible API, they integrate with popular agentic harnesses without extra adapters. Start the vLLM server, then follow the harness-specific instructions below.

OpenCode is an AI coding agent that runs in your terminal.

Configure ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json:

For full documentation, see opencode.ai/docs.

Pi is a minimal agent harness for AI-powered coding that runs in your terminal. It supports custom providers via a models.json configuration file.

Then select the granite-4.2-30b model with /model or Ctrl+L in the interactive session.

OpenHands is an AI software engineer that can plan, write code, and execute commands.

Install and launch OpenHands following the official installation guide.

Configure the LLM in the OpenHands settings with:

Note: The openai/ prefix is required when connecting to OpenAI-compatible endpoints like vLLM. Refer to the OpenHands local LLM documentation for detailed setup instructions, troubleshooting, and alternative installation methods.
