#9659. The 20 Best Local LLMs of 2026: A Complete Guide for Enterprises and Power Users

The | Gen AI | AI Agents | AI Tools | SLMs | LLMs | Engineer | Quantum | Research | Developer | Python | Go | Rust | Mastery Playbook.

The | Gen AI | AI Agents | AI Tools | SLMs | LLMs | Engineer | Quantum | Research | Developer | Python | Go | Rust | Mastery Playbook.

The | Gen AI | AI Agents | AI Tools | SLMs | LLMs | Engineer | Quantum | Research | Developer | Python | Go | Rust | Mastery Playbook.

Your provider changed its usage caps again.

Your legal team will not let customer data touch a third-party API.

Your best engineer hit a rate limit in the middle of a production incident.

Most CTOs, founders and serious AI users have lived at least one of these lines this year.

That is why it’s high time every enterprise worldwide tool Local AI seriously.

Open-weight models crossed a threshold in 2026.

Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM-5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Muse Spark Open and Mistral Large 4 now trade blows with the closed frontier, and every one of them can be downloaded today.

Put the right model on the right hardware, and the token meter simply stops running.

This guide ranks 20 open-weight models in two Top Ten lists.

The first list is for enterprises running four 512 GB Mac Studios joined over Thunderbolt 5 into a 2,048 GB pool of unified memory.

The second is for power users with a single machine and at least 64 GB of VRAM or unified memory.

You will get parameter counts, architectures, published benchmarks, quantized and uncensored Hugging Face releases, a full quantization primer, two detailed budgets, and the security case for running all of this yourself.

If you are interested in Local LLMs, and saving your API bills (or eliminating them entirely) you need to read this!

Cloud AI is priced like electricity from a landlord.

You pay per token, you accept the landlord's rules, and the landlord can change the price whenever it likes.

Local AI turns that per-token bill into a capacity bill you own.

You pay once for hardware, then a modest amount for power, and the marginal cost of the next million tokens is close to zero.

Here is what changes the day your model runs on your own silicon:

Within the throughput of your hardware, yes - and that distinction matters, which is why this guide spends so much time on memory, bandwidth and money.

The core rule of local inference is simple.

Capacity decides which models fit, and bandwidth decides how fast they run.

You cannot talk about local AI without talking about quantization.

It is the single technique that turns a 1.6 terabyte download into something that fits on a desk.

But first - what the heck is quantization anyway?

Every model is a giant collection of numbers called weights. At training time each weight is usually stored in 16-bit or 32-bit floating point.

Quantization stores those same weights with fewer bits. Fewer bits per weight means less memory, less data to move per token, and therefore faster generation on bandwidth-bound hardware like Apple Silicon.

Push the bit count too low and the model starts to forget facts, lose track of long instructions, and make sloppy tool calls.

Add roughly 10 to 30 percent on top for the KV cache, runtime buffers and the operating system.

A 70-billion-parameter model at 4.5 bits per weight needs about 39 GB for weights alone.

The key difference from older 4-bit schemes is quantization-aware training.

When a lab trains the model to live in 4 bits from the start, the quality loss largely disappears.

GGUF is the file format of llama.cpp, and by extension Ollama, LM Studio and Jan. Its quant names look cryptic, but they follow a pattern.

The "K" means super-blocks with nested scales, and the S, M and L suffixes mean small, medium and large. The M and L variants keep sensitive tensors such as attention and output layers at higher precision.

When you see "i1-GGUF" in a repository name, such as the mradermacher releases, that means imatrix-calibrated files.

Unsloth's Dynamic 2.0 quants (names like UD-Q4_K_XL or UD-IQ1_S) do not give every layer the same precision.

They keep critical layers at higher bit widths and crush the bulk of the MoE experts harder.

That is how Unsloth lists a 1-bit Mistral Large 4 at about 233 GB and a 1-bit Kimi K3 at about 594 GB, as reported in an M5 Ultra hosting guide.

Unsloth itself claims around 91 percent top-1 agreement for its smallest Mistral Large 4 quant, which is a vendor claim, so test it on your own prompts.

Apple's MLX framework has its own group-wise quantization at 3, 4, 6 and 8 bits, published under the mlx-community organisation on Hugging Face.

On Apple Silicon, MLX is often noticeably faster than llama.cpp for the same model.

One measured comparison on an M5 Ultra found DeepSeek V4 Flash at about 40 tokens per second under llama.cpp and about 53 tokens per second under MLX, according to an M5 Ultra benchmark.

That is roughly a third more speed from a software switch.

The KV cache stores the attention keys and values for every token in your context.

At a million tokens of context it can rival the weights in size.

Both llama.cpp and MLX can store the KV cache in 8-bit or 4-bit.

An 8-bit KV cache is nearly free in quality and halves context memory, while 4-bit is more aggressive and worth testing on long-document tasks first.

DeepSeek says V4.1 Flash cuts its KV cache to about a quarter of V4 Flash's, and hybrid linear-attention designs like Qwen's Gated DeltaNet and Kimi's Delta Attention shrink it further.

Dense models below 40B: stay at Q5_K_M or higher.

Mid-size MoE models: Q4_K_M or MLX 4-bit.

Trillion-parameter MoE models: whatever fits, because a 2-bit giant often beats an 8-bit dwarf.

They come straight out of the file sizes of the models that matter in late 2026.

Kimi K3.1 Pro is a 2.8-trillion-parameter model that downloads at about 1.56 TB in its native MXFP4 format, as confirmed in a Kimi K3.1 Pro weights report.

Mistral Large 4 is about 1,060 GB in official FP8, and Muse Spark Open needs about 1.63 TB in full BF16.

A single 512 GB Mac Studio cannot hold any of these at high precision.

Two machines (1,024 GB) hold some of them at 4-bit.

Four machines (2,048 GB) hold every one of them at its native or near-native precision, with room left over.

That headroom is not waste. It goes to three jobs:

Four is also the natural size for a Thunderbolt 5 mesh.

Each Mac Studio can cable directly to the other three, so every node is one hop from every other node, and there is no switch to buy or fail.

Apple added RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 in macOS 26.2, and Jeff Geerling's cluster test showed exo with RDMA speeding up as nodes were added while llama.cpp over TCP slowed down.

On Qwen3 235B, exo went from 19.5 tokens per second on one node to 31.9 on four, according to AppleInsider's write-up.

With the 2026 M5 Ultra, each node brings 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth.

Four of them reach about 4.8 TB/s in aggregate, a figure exo Labs highlights in its four Mac cluster announcement.

Why 512 GB nodes rather than eight 256 GB nodes?

TechRepublic notes that two 256 GB Mac Studios cost about $700 less than one 512 GB machine, so smaller nodes are cheaper per gigabyte.

But eight nodes cannot form a direct mesh, every extra hop adds synchronisation latency, and every extra box adds cables, power bricks and failure points.

The 2026 mid-size models are astonishingly good.

Qwen3.8-27B posts 61.7 on SWE-bench Pro, and its 4-bit build is only about 17 GB, according to a Qwen3.8-27B analysis.

Because the floor is about running the best small models well, not just running them.

One hundred and twenty-eight is the sweet spot.

Hardware: four Mac Studios with M5 Ultra and 512 GB of unified memory each, cabled as a Thunderbolt 5 mesh with RDMA enabled, for 2,048 GB of pooled memory and about 4.8 TB/s of aggregate bandwidth.

Ranking rule: most powerful in real-world usability first. I weigh output quality, agentic and tool-calling reliability, speed on this cluster, licence freedom and context length - not raw benchmark scores alone.

A word on benchmarks: almost every number below is vendor-reported, and labs use different harnesses. Treat cross-lab comparisons as directional, not as gospel.

Moonshot AI's Kimi K3.1 Pro is the most capable open-weight model you can download as of late November 2026.

Why rank 1: nothing else open-weight matches its combination of agentic depth, million-token context and multimodal input. It is the slowest model on this list - and the smartest.

Z.ai's GLM-5.3 is the coding and cybersecurity specialist of the open frontier.

If your enterprise writes software, this is the model your engineers will fight over.

Its successor, GLM-5.4, arrived on 23 November as Z.ai's first Loop Transformer, running 28 layers of the GLM-5 base twice at about 750B parameters.

It is hosted-only for now, Z.ai has published no benchmark scores for it, and weights will follow safety hardening, per The Next Web.

Until they ship, GLM-5.3 is the GLM you can own.

Why rank 2: on coding and terminal work it sits right next to the closed frontier, it runs faster than Kimi because only 40B parameters are active, and its licence is practically unrestricted.

DeepSeek did something unusual in September 2026.

It released a "Flash" model and then retired its own flagship because the Flash model beat it.

Why rank 3: MIT licence, million-token context, vision, and near-frontier agentic scores at a fraction of the active compute. It is the model that serves the most people per watt.

Inkling 2 Small is the newest model on this list, and it replaces Inkling-Small outright. Thinking Machines built it as a base for agents that plan, call tools and check their own results - chat quality came second.

Why rank 4: Apache 2.0 weights, a million-token context, vision and agentic scores just behind DeepSeek V4.1 Flash - all at 17B active. It is the strongest permissively licensed agent model on this list.

Alibaba's Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B is the open-weight release of Qwen3.8-Max, and the first time Qwen has opened a Max-tier model.

Why rank 5: enormous knowledge capacity and strong reasoning, held back from a higher rank only by the text-only open checkpoint and the need to quantize it.

Mistral Large 4, nicknamed "Le Chonk", is Europe's trillion-parameter answer, trained from scratch on Mistral's own European infrastructure.

Why rank 6: a trillion-parameter model with a clean commercial licence for in-house use and the strongest sovereignty story in this list for European buyers.

Meta's Muse Spark Open is the most capable US open-weight model to date, and it was built with the Mac Studio in mind.

Why rank 7: the fastest measured giant on this exact hardware and the best tool-user in the list, held back by its licence and by trailing the top three on hard coding.

Thinking Machines Lab, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, released Inkling as a broad, balanced base for enterprises to shape themselves.

Why rank 8: Apache 2.0, audio input and a design built for customisation make it the deepest foundation for a proprietary in-house model, though the newer Inkling 2 Small is the better pick if you do not need audio.

MiniMax M3 is the long-context efficiency specialist of the group.

Why rank 9: the most efficient million-token model here, small enough to run on a single node at 4-bit.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is Alibaba's early preview of the Qwen4 architecture, and it is brutally efficient.

Why rank 10: it does not compete with the giants on depth, but it lets one cluster serve hundreds of quick requests while the giants think.

Inkling-Small (276B, 12B active, about 552 GB in BF16), now superseded by Inkling 2 Small but still a light fine-tuning base, per the Inkling-Small model card; GLM-5.4 (about 750B), which is live on Z.ai's Coding Plan but has no open weights yet; GLM-5.3-Flash (320B, 18B active), NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL (120B, 12B active), and Meituan's LongCat-2.5 (1.6T, about 48B active, MIT), whose model card currently documents deployment only on NPUs.

Hardware: one system with at least 64 GB of VRAM or unified memory. Think Ryzen AI Max+ 395 mini PCs, NVIDIA DGX Spark, M5 Max or M5 Ultra Mac Studios, or a workstation with an RTX PRO 6000.

Ranking rule: usability first. For a single machine that means quality per gigabyte, speed, tool-calling reliability, licence freedom, and the availability of good quantized and uncensored builds.

Memory tier notes: each entry lists the smallest tier that runs it comfortably, so you can see at a glance what your own machine can handle.

The best local model you can run on a single consumer machine in late 2026 is a 27-billion-parameter dense model.

Why rank 1: frontier-class agentic scores, Apache 2.0, a tiny memory footprint, and some of the most downloaded abliterated releases on Hugging Face.

DeepSeek V4 Flash has been retired from DeepSeek's API in favour of V4.1 Flash, but its MIT-licensed weights remain one of the best things a single large-memory machine can run.

Local performance: about 53 tokens per second under MLX and 40 under llama.cpp on an M5 Ultra.

Why rank 2: the strongest MIT-licensed model a single machine can hold at 4-bit. It only drops below Qwen3.8-27B because it needs four to eight times the memory.

Inkling 2 Mini is the smallest model in Thinking Machines' second generation, and it brings a new idea to the desktop: a looped transformer.

Why rank 3: the most agentic capability per gigabyte on this list, with Apache 2.0 weights and a million-token context. It sits behind Qwen3.8-27B, which matches it on the Intelligence Index with a more mature uncensored ecosystem, and behind DeepSeek V4 Flash on raw depth.

Google DeepMind's Gemma 4 31B is the strongest Western dense model you can run on a laptop-class machine.

Why rank 4: outstanding reasoning per gigabyte and a mature uncensored ecosystem, but weaker than Qwen on agentic software engineering, scoring 52.0 on SWE-bench Verified in Qwen's comparison table.

OpenAI's gpt-oss-120b is more than a year old, and it is still on this list. That tells you how well it was built.

Why rank 5: rock-solid tool calling and the most battle-tested uncensored variants in the list, held back by a shorter context window and its age.

Mistral Small 4 is three models in one: Magistral reasoning, Pixtral vision and Devstral coding, merged into a single MoE.

Why rank 6: the most versatile single model at this size, with a configurable reasoning effort that keeps answers short when you want speed.

Three billion active parameters should not be able to do this.

Why rank 7: the best speed-to-intelligence ratio in the power-user list.

The largest Apache-licensed Qwen MoE that fits comfortably in 128 GB.

Why rank 8: best-in-class tool use for its size, though the newer Qwen3.8-27B now beats it on coding.

Meta's return to open weights started small, and small turned out to be very good.

Why rank 9: a strong American Apache-licensed option that beats Gemma 4 31B on software engineering, though Qwen still leads on terminal and computer-use work.

NVIDIA squeezed a 74-billion-parameter agent model into 24 GB. On a 64 GB machine that leaves an enormous budget for context.

Why rank 10: the fastest agent in the list on NVIDIA hardware, but its intelligence index trails the Qwen and Gemma models above it.

Gemma 4 26B A4B (25.2B, 3.8B active, Apache 2.0), still brilliant at reasoning per watt but weak at agentic coding, with imatrix GGUFs from mradermacher of its abliterated build; Devstral Small 2 (24B, Apache 2.0, a focused local coding agent), Olmo 3.1 32B (fully open training data), and Inkling 2 Small for anyone with a 512 GB machine, where bartowski's Q4_K_M build (about 369 GB) fits with room for context.

Memory figures marked with a tilde are approximate weight sizes from model cards, quant repositories and the guides cited above, before KV cache. "n/a" means no published figure I could verify.

Prices below are US list prices as of November 2026; items marked "estimate" are my planning figures, not quotes, so get real quotes before you buy.

Apple measured time to first token on a 65,536-token context falling from about 50.5 seconds to 40.6 seconds when it used two cables per link instead of one, per MIXED's Muse Spark report.

Cables are the cheapest speed-up you will ever buy.

LLM Reference lists Kimi K3.1 Pro at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

Closed frontier models cost far more; DeepSeek's V4-Pro launch price, for example, was reported at roughly a twentieth of Opus 4.7's.

A four-node cluster running Kimi K3.1 Pro generates in the mid-teens of tokens per second per stream, so heavy volume has to be spread across the faster models in the list, such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, MiniMax M3 and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

The HTML edition of this article in my personal blog includes a calculator so you can plug in your own numbers.

The power-user budget is a ladder. Climb as high as your models need, and no higher.

Sources: the 64 GB Framework price from Notebookcheck's price report and the 128 GB price from Phoronix's Framework coverage; DGX Spark and Mac Studio M5 Max prices from ComputingForGeeks' hardware guide; the AMD Ryzen AI Halo from Tom's Hardware; the 256 GB Mac Studio price is derived from TechRepublic's note that two 256 GB units cost $21,598; RTX PRO 6000 pricing from Tom's DGX Spark launch coverage.

Memory prices have been volatile in 2026, so check before you buy.

If all you need is Qwen3.8-27B, its hosted API costs about $0.20 per million input tokens and $2.50 per million output tokens on LLM Reference.

Light users will never recover a $3,600 machine through token savings alone.

But heavy agentic coders are not light users.

If you push 300 million input tokens and 30 million output tokens a month through a frontier API priced like Kimi K3.1 Pro, that is about $900 a month, and a $3,449 Framework Desktop with 128 GB pays for itself in about four months - provided the local model is good enough for the job.

The real return for power users is not only the money.

It is uncensored models when you need them.

These are the problems I care about most, and they are exactly where cloud AI pricing breaks down.

This section explains why I chose a 2 TB unified memory setup, and why the reason is not chat - it is coordinated teams of 100 or more agents.

Research on open problems is not one clever prompt.

It is thousands of attempts, most of them failures, each re-reading long contexts full of definitions, prior attempts and formal proof states.

When I first wrote this section, I said no AI system had solved a Millennium Prize Problem.

Here is what happened in the autumn of 2026.

Read the dates carefully, because every claim below is still waiting on human review.

The Riemann result had a quieter prelude.

In August, a research version of Claude raised the proven share of zeta zeros on the critical line from 41.6 percent to 67.2 percent, per Anthropic's zeta note - real progress, but not a proof.

The Millennium Prize list on Wikipedia now marks the Riemann Hypothesis and Navier-Stokes as "solution claimed; prize pending".

The Clay Institute has awarded nothing yet, and P vs NP remains open.

Now look at how every one of these results was produced.

That is exactly the workload this section is about.

And ten thousand agents is a cloud bill, not a hobby: at even a tenth of the per-agent token volume I assume below, a swarm that size would cost about $130,000 a day at GPT-5.6 Sol prices (my estimate).

The token volumes are my own planning assumptions; the prices are published list prices.

And that is before prompt caching discounts, retries, failed runs, or the inevitable moment someone leaves a swarm running over a long weekend.

The four-node cluster costs about $96,000 in hardware (see the budget section).

After that, the marginal cost of research is mostly electricity.

Mixed load (estimate): about 1 kW for the cluster, or 8,760 kWh a year - roughly $1,300 a year at $0.15 per kWh, or about ₹70,000 at ₹8 per kWh.

So the first year of local research costs about $100,000 all in, against $1.8 million to $9.1 million for the same token volume in the cloud.

Every year after that costs a few thousand dollars of power.

That is the difference between a research programme you can sustain for a decade and one you can afford for a quarter.

A 100-agent team needs three things at once: strong lead reasoners, fast workers, and room for every agent's working context.

One 512 GB machine forces you to pick one of those.

Here is the memory plan I use for a "swarm" configuration on 2,048 GB:

That leaves roughly 6 GB of working memory per agent for a team of 100, before KV cache quantization stretches it further.

For a "deep" configuration, swap the whole roster for Kimi K3.1 Pro (about 1.56 TB) and run a small team of very strong agents instead.

Is 100 agents realistic on four Mac Studios?

Research agents spend much of their time waiting on tools - Lean proof checks, Python experiments, quantum simulators, literature search - so far fewer than 100 are generating tokens at any instant.

The fast, small-active workers (8B to 16B active for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, 6B for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) carry the volume, and the heavy reasoners are called only when a decision needs them.

Agent swarms at this scale are already real.

Moonshot pushed its Agent Swarm to 300 sub-agents running 4,000 coordinated steps with Kimi K2.6, per a Kimi K2.6 report.

A team of 100 agents without structure is just 100 expensive random walks.

The coordination layer is what turns a swarm into a research group.

Quantum research has its own memory hunger.

A full state-vector simulation stores 2ⁿ complex amplitudes at 16 bytes each:

So a single 512 GB node can hold a 34-qubit state vector with room to spare, while the agent team searches error-correcting codes, circuit compilations and variational ansätze around it.

Tensor-network and stabilizer simulators go much further for structured circuits, and the same agents can write and run them.

Will a 100-agent team on four Mac Studios settle P vs NP?

You would need 10,000+ to 100,000+ agents for that. Maybe even 1 million agents.

But can it solve research level problems for your own company?

I strongly believe the people who make progress on the hardest problems will be the ones who can afford to fail ten thousand times.

Local hardware turns failure from a line item into a habit - and that is how business research and new scientific discoveries have always worked.

AI sovereignty means you, your company or your country can keep using AI on your own terms, no matter what a vendor, a regulator abroad or a supply shock decides.

Owning the weights and the hardware is the most direct way to get there.

It is also the only way to ensure your company is running irrespective of internet outages, natural disasters, international calamities or war.

I am not a lawyer, and you should get legal advice for your jurisdiction.

But I strongly believe that every serious organisation should hold at least one capable model it controls completely.

A local model on a badly managed machine is just a new place for data to leak.

The supply chain is the most overlooked risk.

While researching this article I saw dozens of unofficial re-uploads of flagship models from accounts that have nothing to do with the original labs.

Ransomware is moving laterally through your network.

Your analyst pastes an obfuscated PowerShell loader into an AI assistant and asks what it does.

Safety-tuned models are trained to refuse requests that look like hacking.

The trouble is that defending against an attack looks exactly like studying one.

Those are reasonable choices for public chatbots.

But in an incident room, a false refusal can cost you minutes, and minutes are what separate a contained incident from a company-wide outage.

At the same time, capability is clearly there.

GLM-5.3 scores 84.5 on CyberGym, a vulnerability-discovery benchmark, on its model card.

The knowledge exists inside these models; alignment decides whether your defenders can reach it.

An uncensored local model does all of this without arguing, without sending your malware samples or breach details to a third party, and without a rate limit in the middle of the night.

During a breach, you may not be able to trust your own network, your SaaS accounts or your internet connection.

A model running on an isolated Mac Studio or a disconnected workstation keeps working when everything else is suspect.

And sending live incident data to an external API during a breach is a disclosure decision your legal team should make deliberately - not something an analyst should do at 3 a.m. by accident.

Uncensored models are powerful tools, so treat them like any other powerful tool.

Isolate the machine on a dedicated analysis network with no route to production.

Log every prompt and response for later review.

Write an acceptable-use policy that covers defensive work, authorised testing scope and prohibited uses.

Keep an aligned model for everyone else. The uncensored model belongs in the security toolkit, not on every desk.

Vet the abliterated build using the provenance checklist above.

The community already publishes hundreds of abliterated models, browsable in catalogues such as Featherless's abliterated catalogue, including some aimed at security work, but you must test any such model yourself.

Good news - the defenders now have frontier-grade help that never says no.

Bad news - so do the attackers, which is exactly why your team cannot afford to work with one hand tied behind its back.

Software decides whether you actually enjoy using it.

You just told me a 128 GB box will never pay for itself if I only use Qwen3.8-27B lightly.

You told me a four-node cluster generates Kimi K3.1 Pro at the speed of a fast typist.

Cloud APIs for open models are cheap, they scale instantly, and someone else patches the servers.

With Cloud APIs, I do not need to pay for upgrades and maintenance.

2 TB is overkill for most small businesses.

But cost per token was never the whole story.

You cannot rent sovereignty, you cannot rent an air gap, and you cannot rent a model that will help you dissect ransomware at 3 a.m. without logging your breach on someone else's server.

The same kind of four-Mac Studio cluster that ran Kimi K2 Thinking in late 2025 runs far more capable models today, because the models keep getting more efficient while the hardware you already own stays paid for.

Run the private, sensitive, high-volume and always-on work locally, and keep a cloud API for the rare task that needs the biggest closed model.

Will the cloud API survive a war in your country?

If the AI bubble pops, where will you get your AI?

If all leading AI labs increase costs to cover their bills, what will you do with your current budget?

If your country is listed as opposition to the USA, where is your frontier level AI?

If your company is banned by mistake, what will you do?

If your infrastructure goes down, and you are running a mission-critical business, where is your backup?

If one of your systems are hacked, how will you fight back? Will you feed sensitive company data into foreign servers?

If your system requires cyberattack analysis, how will you bypass safeguards on US AI Companies?

Will you end up sending your sensitive data to Chinese servers, which are regulated by the Chinese government?

These are the reasons why every company on earth needs local LLMs!

Especially in the current geopolitical situation!

Two years ago, running a frontier-class model at home was a stunt.

Four Mac Studios give an enterprise 2,048 GB of unified memory and the freedom to run Kimi K3.1 Pro, GLM-5.3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Inkling 2 Small, Qwen3.8, Mistral Large 4 and Muse Spark Open on its own terms.

A single 64 to 128 GB machine gives a power user Qwen3.8-27B, Inkling 2 Mini, Gemma 4, gpt-oss-120b and Mistral Small 4 - with uncensored builds a download away.

Where will you be when the next price change lands?

Where will you be when the next outage hits?

Where will you be when the next breach starts at 3 a.m.?

The organisations that own their intelligence will move faster, sleep better and defend harder than the ones that rent it.

Especially with uncensored models (with strict access rules!) when cyber-attacks are a real and active threat.

By God's grace, the future of AI is open, local and yours.

And if you are building your AI strategy right now - start with one machine, one model, and one sensitive workflow you will never send to the cloud again.

The best way to build a Local AI system is in modules, one machine at a time, not a big bang!

I am working as a Generative AI Consultant available for work globally, on a remote basis.

I have 500+ publications across 10+ platforms covering AI, agentic systems, quantum computing, LLMs, Local AI, and other emerging technologies, for which I acts as a consultant in Python, Go, Rust, and the Claude AI Ecosystem and the Gemini AI Ecosystem.

Find my work at my personal blog thomascherickal.com and my business consulting website thedigitalfuturist.com.

#9657. Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:

No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: How to Kill the Code Review

Nov 26, 2026 2 min read

Closing the Engineering the Developer Experience track at QCon San Francisco 2026, Ankit Jain, co-founder and CEO of Aviator, argued that line-by-line code review is already quietly dead on most teams, and that the sharper question is "how long until we stop reading the code?" He also flagged his conflict of interest up front, noting that he runs a company that sells a solution and asking the audience to "be suspicious of me."

The talk revisited an essay he wrote for Latent Space in March 2026 proposing a five-layer trust model to replace reviews. Eight months on, Jain said the mechanics held up but the essay missed human judgment entirely. He began with the data that unseated his original framing. A 2013 Microsoft study found 44% of reviewers cited defect-finding as their motivation, yet only 14% of their comments were actually about defects, and a 2018 Google study of more than nine million reviews reached almost the same split. Code review was never really about bugs, he argued, it was about knowledge sharing, echoing Addy Osmani: "We made writing cheap, and understanding stayed exactly as expensive as it has always been."

A September Faros study of more than 4,000 teams found that over 75% of PRs now merge without any human review, average PR size has grown, and redo work is up 67% year over year. Earlier research showed review quality drops sharply past 400 lines, yet the median PR today is 640 lines. "We are reviewing the code, but we are rubber stamping it," Jain said, pointing to a Reddit post from an experienced developer refusing to review AI-generated PRs that collected over 1,900 upvotes. The result is "review theater," where agents write, another AI reviews, agents revise, and humans skim and merge.

To replace a single review, Jain proposed six layers: Argue, Capture, Codify, Prove, Debate, Own. Agents should argue about a change locally before the PR exists, surfacing only what they disagreed about. Intent and acceptance criteria, familiar from behaviour-driven development, should be captured during the coding session and attached to the PR rather than discarded. Repeated review comments become invariants, standing rules with scope, provenance, a verification method, and a team owner. Aviator mined 11,000 of its own review comments to produce 64 invariants. Evidence should replace green checks: screenshots, DOM snapshots, recorded requests, latencies, and database logs, because the same agent that wrote the code likely wrote its unit tests. Humans then debate decisions rather than diffs, and ownership shifts from author and reviewer to the teams that own the rules.

Jain reported his nine-engineer team now merges four times the PRs it did a year ago and still approves every one, while reverts have dropped around 40%. He also shared a failure: a change passed every filter and caused an 18-minute outage from an unindexed query, after which the post-mortem asked which rule was missing rather than who approved it. Critical areas such as security, authentication and billing still get line-by-line review.

He closed with a line: You can outsource your thinking. You cannot outsource your understanding.

#9654. Industrial Serial Gateways Broadcast That They're Insecure

Critical OT access devices will often tell you, and anyone else, whether they're protected by authentication — and many aren't.

Internet scans indicate that some substantial fraction of serial device servers deployed at operational technology (OT) sites worldwide not only lack authentication but also broadcast the fact publicly.

We all have a friend or a family member who's deeply insecure, and it's obvious as soon as they start talking. The same can be said of serial-to-IP gateways. Recently, Adrian Cheek, senior cybercrime researcher for Flare, probed the wider Internet for these sorts of devices, finding that a substantial chunk of them are discoverable. Worse, they often responded to straightforward requests by saying whether they were or were not protected by authentication — and many were not.

An insecure serial-to-IP gateway is a serious risk to anyone downstream of it. These devices are responsible for translating information between the Internet and industrial machinery. So in a cyberattack, a reachable and unauthenticated one can inadvertently translate an Internet-based threat into one that affects major, safety-critical machines.

Related:How to Assess OT Incident Response Preparedness

Using a specific vendor's UDP discovery service, rather than probing all vendors' devices, Cheek found 2,474 serial-to-IP gateways exposed on the Web. They seemed to map to real devices rather than honeypots, with half of them located in Russia.

For some reason, in response to the researcher's unsolicited probes, around half of the devices — 1,265 — proffered their authentication status. Of those that did, 973 reported that authentication was disabled. In other words, 39.3% of all Internet-exposed gateways visibly lacked authentication, and among those whose status could be gleaned, that figure was 77%.

"These devices ship with authentication off. An integrator sets one up on a bench, gets the meter or the drive or the Remote Terminal Unit (RTU) talking to the SCADA host, and moves on to the next site," Cheek laments. "The device then does one job for 10 or 15 years, and nobody logs into it again. In many cases, the operator doesn't even know it exists because it went in as part of someone else's equipment."

There are also understandable, if not entirely justifiable, reasons why operators fail to conceal and lock down their serial device servers. Cheek cites a multitude of reasons, including that enabling such security features can break software on the host side.

"Older SCADA packages and virtual serial port drivers may not support the secured modes, so an operator who switches them on can lose the link to the field," he says. "Then someone has to drive to an unstaffed site to fix it. Firmware updates carry the same risk at a remote site with no spare on hand. People who have been burned by that once are slow to touch a working device again."

Related:Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

Still, an exposed, unauthenticated serial gateway is a welcome mat for bad actors. Not only does it give arbitrary actors entry into sensitive OT systems and eliminate the need to exploit any kind of vulnerabilities, it also allows attackers to use the vendor's own supplied tools, which could blend malicious activity in with normal IT-OT traffic.

Cheek made special mention of the risk to mobile network operators and, even more specifically, private access point name (APN) service providers. Last year's Polish power grid attack used a private APN to pivot from a wind farm's network to the power plant where the attackers ultimately shut down a steam turbine, water treatment system, and seven serial-to-IP devices. According to Flare, 322 of the 2,474 discovered devices in the study lived in address space associated with known mobile network operators in Europe and the Middle East.

OT operators can begin to secure their OT access layer by first doing an inventory of the devices they're running. "For every cellular unit, find out what plan the SIM is on and whether it gets a public address. Then ask your carrier in writing whether devices on your private network can reach each other or devices belonging to other customers," Cheek notes. "Don't assume the managed product isolates them. In the Polish incident, that missing isolation is what let the attacker move between two unrelated organizations."

Related:Fresh European Fridge Attacks Put Cold-Chain Security in Focus

Next, he advises, "Lock down the data ports as well as the login. Most of these devices let you restrict which IP addresses can open a connection. Configure them so only the SCADA host can reach the serial ports and only an engineering workstation can reach the management interface. Switch off the services you don't use, which on most units means the discovery service, Telnet, older SNMP, and often the Web interface. Remove SSH and Telnet entirely from anything that faces the carrier network," and plop a strict firewall between the gateway and control network.

There are also general practices organizations can put in place, like ensuring that the next time they purchase serial device servers, a person or team is assigned to be responsible for the devices, and that they have necessary credentials, configuration, and network details from system integrators.

At the end of the day, though, nothing compares to preventing an attacker's ability to find and speak to a device in the first place.

"Even a fully patched gateway with authentication on is usually connected to equipment on the serial side that has no security of its own," Cheek points out. "A meter, a drive, or an RTU will accept any correctly formed command that reaches it. So the useful question is who can reach the gateway at all, because whoever can reach it gets whatever is behind it. Authentication and patching both matter, but restricting what can reach the gateway does more good than either."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9653. Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

#9651. 6 Ways to Disagree With Someone Without Damaging the Relationship

Author Upgrade Your Mindset, Rethink Imposter Syndrome. Scaling products ￫ Scaling thinking. Former AVP Engg @Swiggy

Author Upgrade Your Mindset, Rethink Imposter Syndrome. Scaling products ￫ Scaling thinking. Former AVP Engg @Swiggy

Author Upgrade Your Mindset, Rethink Imposter Syndrome. Scaling products ￫ Scaling thinking. Former AVP Engg @Swiggy

Most of us find it hard to speak up at work and it gets even more challenging when we aren’t just sharing an idea, but refuting someone else’s viewpoint. Becoming too eager to tell others they’re wrong can invite pushback and make others dismiss or disregard your thinking. Attacking their intelligence or motives, acting mean or belittling them in any way can put them on the defensive and kill any chance you had to find a better solution. When others feel judged, misunderstood or unsupported, they feel unsafe which makes them more cautious, watchful and guarded. Instead of handling the disagreement with openness and curiosity, they try to protect themselves by retaliating, arguing or becoming disengaged.

Keeping quiet and not speaking up is also not an option because holding your thoughts and not sharing them can lead to bad choices and poor decisions. It can result in missed opportunities, mediocre solutions and terrible mistakes. Not contributing to the discussion with the fear of how it will be perceived or worrying about damaging the relationship keeps you safe, but it also prevents you from embracing discomfort, which is necessary for growth.

Disagreeing with others in a way that does not increase tension, make the other person feel attacked, criticized or lead to defensive and argumentative behavior requires kind clarity—being direct and honest while maintaining empathy and compassion. It requires delivering honest opinions without sugar-coating, while ensuring they feel respected and valued. It requires challenging them while continuing to be supportive.

People often silence themselves, or "agree to disagree" without fully exploring the actual nature of the disagreement, for the sake of protecting a relationship and maintaining connection. But when we avoid certain conversations, and never fully learn how the other person feels about all of the issues, we sometimes end up making assumptions that not only perpetuate but deepen misunderstandings, and that can generate resentment.

Follow these practices to show maturity by disagreeing with others without being disrespectful.

When you find a flaw in someone’s argument, notice their mistake or have better suggestions on how something must be done, you may be tempted to interrupt and insert your opinion. But speaking up and disagreeing before giving an opportunity to another person to complete their thoughts or making them feel heard and understood leaves them feeling frustrated, doubted and attacked. Their instant reaction is to oppose, resist and fight back without evaluating your idea or suggestion.

Listening on the other hand, without expressing your disapproval in either words or body language, makes others feel trusted and respected. It creates an environment of psychological safety, clarifies your intent and sets the tone of the conversation that you’re not there to judge, impose or make them feel inferior.

To listen effectively, stop showing an eagerness to disagree:

Genuine listening means suspending memory, desire, and judgement and, for a few moments at least, existing for the other person.

When you speak to someone you disagree with, recognize their ideas and feelings first—show that what they have to say matters.

Words used to convey disagreement plays a crucial role in how your message is perceived—whether others are receptive to your viewpoint or they outrightly reject it. Using words that come across as  judgmental or too opinionated or using language that’s disrespectful or sarcastic makes disagreement less about finding the best path forward and more about ego—protecting one’s self-respect and self-esteem. Offending others by passing personal remarks or trying to prove they’re wrong activates their amygdala, which triggers fight-flight-freeze response, turning an already difficult situation into an impossible one.

Avoiding words that have the potential to be misinterpreted, stating your views without making it personal or coming across too strong and expressing your concerns in a non-judgmental neutral tone can invite others to take your opinion seriously. They may engage with you to better understand your perspective, show curiosity to dig deeper and think more clearly, leading to a highly constructive discussion.

When sharing your disagreement, using certain words is a big no-no. They trigger intense negative feelings which puts others on the defensive:

We cannot control the way people interpret our ideas or thoughts, but we can control the words and tones we choose to convey them. Peace is built on understanding, and wars are built on misunderstandings. Never underestimate the power of a single word, and never recklessly throw around words.

When you speak to someone you disagree with, think carefully about the effect of what you say and avoid emotionally charged words which makes the conversation ineffective.

When you don’t agree with someone or have a different point of view, you may rush with an opinion, jump to conclusions or become impatient to get yourself heard. Being too direct can make you come across as pushy, rude, inconsiderate, insensitive and controlling. Directly stating your opinion without taking the time to understand their thinking—what are their beliefs, what matters to them, how did they reach this decision—can make you try very hard to get yourself heard, but your voice will never reach or get across to them.

Questioning, on the other hand, not only gets you closer to their perspective, it makes others feel valued and respected. When you show curiosity to understand others, they reciprocate in kind—your inputs don’t invite pushback, but are treated as an opportunity to explore, test and learn. Questions unlock thinking, gets you closer to differences of opinion and challenges you to reconsider your own point of view without considering it as the only option worthy of time and attention.

Seek clarity and invite others to talk by asking open ended questions:

Questioning helps people gain perspective and understand the perspectives of others. As they see issues and problems from different points of view, they gain an appreciation for their complexity—and also expand the range of possible solutions.

When you speak to someone you disagree with, use questions to find common ground, uncover patterns and help others see the gaps in their thinking instead of stating it explicitly.

When you don’t agree with someone, you may feel compelled to change their mind by imposing your thoughts and trying to micromanage the outcome. You may attack their thoughts and beliefs, present strong evidence to prove they’re wrong and push aggressively to make them see the issue differently. Trying to change someone’s mind is a cognitive shift—years of ingrained beliefs and attitudes are hard to change because they’re tied to identity, ego and biases, making others “dig in” rather than change. When people feel their beliefs are being attacked, the conversation shifts from problem-solving to winning. The more you push, the more fixed those beliefs can become. Trying to change someone’s mind can also come across as corrective—they may feel you don’t respect their thinking, trust their judgment or that your perspective matters more than their point of view.

Trying to influence others on the other hand, is a behavioral shift—it involves discussing actions, priorities, risks, incentives or trade-offs to help others make a better decision in the moment regardless of their original belief. Influence is achieved through framing—What are the trade-offs? What are the second-order effects? What happens if we do nothing? The idea is to guide their thinking, not impose yours.

The key word in our definition of a disagreement (an unacceptable difference between two perspectives), isn’t “difference.” It’s “unacceptable.” Once the clash between perspectives becomes unacceptable, our motivation shifts from understanding minds to changing them, and from that shift springs a world of trouble.

When you speak to someone you disagree with, focusing on changing their mind can make you less influential as they feel managed and intellectually overpowered. Rather, explore together, invite reflection and try to expand their perspective instead of changing their belief.

Disagreements often turn unproductive and spiral out of control when conversations go off-track and lose focus. Finger-pointing, blame games and other irrelevant points of discussion divert attention away from the main goal. Giving in and contributing to these emotional outbursts by sharing your own frustrations, disappointment or other concerns can waste everyone’s time and energy while not taking you any closer to your goals. Participating in unrelated topics or disconnected arguments derails you from discussing the main idea and making progress on reaching a mutual conclusion.

Remaining present and calm during the emotional moments, reminding everyone of the end goal and tactfully bringing the conversation back to the agenda can unlock clearer thinking, more rational arguments and a better aligned decision. It can pave the path to disagree and commit—disagree and commit divulges the importance of commitment despite our differences. At its core, it supports unity, maturity to disconnect our identity from our ideas and support others even when we do not agree with their point of view. It doesn’t hide the fact that we disagree nor dismiss the value of our opinion, it simply guides us to know when it’s time to get past our convictions and work with others instead of working against them. Reiterating the end goal recenters the discussion on shared purpose instead of competing opinions.

Respect for the problem places all that we're struggling with into the landscape of the conversation itself. It lets us step back and take a satellite view of the way our tough conversation is playing out. The conversation is no longer a battlefield, but a course of obstacles through which we move.

When you speak to someone you disagree with, discuss what’s relevant to the current conversation. Stay on track. Avoid going off-topic.

Some disagreements may never get resolved, not because you’re doing something wrong or you’re being unreasonable. However, despite your best efforts you may not be able to influence others or reach a conclusion. In some cases, disagreeing with someone superior to you or those in positions of power can even backfire—they may hold it against you which can impact your career and growth. People who display extreme insecurity, stubbornness, egotism or narcissism are often hard to disagree with because they do not want a productive conversation—they want to feel superior, in control and right. They will portray you as a difficult person to discredit your viewpoint. They enjoy arguing for the sake of winning and always take the opposite side regardless of what you say. They consider themselves as the smartest person in the room and belittle you to assert their superiority.

When disagreement feels like a battle or starts to impact your mental health and personal well-being, it’s wise to emotionally detach yourself and walk away from it. Nothing in this world is worth your sanity. It’s important to voice your opinion and share your thoughts, but when the conversation crosses the safe boundary and enters into an unhealthy zone, staying in it or letting yourself be bothered about it is a foolish thing to do. Ruminating about it or spending more time and energy into fixing the situation may only make it harder to let it go.

To identify if you should walk away from a disagreement:

Reason tells us that we should always be able to work things out with words. But the absurdly profound truth is that in many crucial moments of conflict, when sanity and safety hang in the balance, choosing not to engage verbally can be by far the most powerful form of speech.

Not all disagreements need to be resolved and not all of them are worthy. Knowing the difference is crucial to be effective without losing your mind.

7 Ways to Build Stronger Relationships at Work

#9649. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.
