#9634. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

#9633. Satellites Have a Ground-Level Cybersecurity Problem

Weaknesses in the ground-based infrastructure supporting satellite services are becoming more consequential as a new space race gathers pace.

The satellites circling Earth may seem far removed from the reach of cyberattackers, but the ground-based networks and infrastructure supporting them have long offered plenty of ways in. That exposure is now becoming increasingly consequential as the number of satellites in orbit and the services depending on them grow rapidly.

In a new analysis of cyber threats emerging around the booming space ecosystem, Recorded Future's Insikt Group warned that in 2025 alone, organizations and nations around the world placed 4,517 satellites in orbit; 87% of them are commercially owned, contributing to a $686 billion space economy that is growing rapidly.

Satellite services now underpin a growing range of everyday services and critical operations, from communications and navigation to shipping and infrastructure monitoring. As dependence on them grows, so does the potential fallout from a cyberattack that disrupts them, Recorded Future researchers warned. The growing militarization of space and the emergence of orbital AI data centers, such as those that Google and SpaceX are exploring with Project Suncatcher and Starmind, respectively, introduce another layer of risk, the company said.

Related:It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

Recorded Future pointed to several incidents where attackers exploited weaknesses in the ground-based systems supporting satellite communications to cause widespread disruption. One of the most consequential examples was in February 2022, just before Russia invaded Ukraine. Russian attackers used a destructive, data-wiping malware, dubbed AcidRain, to disable tens of thousands of modems connected to Viasat's KA-SAT satellite broadband network, after first gaining access to the network through a misconfigured VPN appliance. The disruption affected Ukrainian military communications as well as ordinary customers across Europe. In Germany, some 5,800 wind turbines lost their remote monitoring connections.

A similar pattern emerged in attacks against Iran's commercial shipping fleet in 2025, when a group calling itself Lab-Dookhtegan disabled communications aboard dozens of tankers and cargo vessels. The attackers reportedly gained access through Fanava Group, an Iranian IT provider serving the fleet, and obtained administrator-level control of shipboard Linux systems. They used that access to disable satellite communications software and software for identifying and tracking ship movements.

Recorded Future also pointed to an incident last August, where an oil tanker lost communications for about 30 hours after attackers seemingly compromised the ship's onboard network. Investigators focused on the satellite terminals aboard the ship and the remote-maintenance systems connecting them to shore as possible points of entry, the company noted.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

"In none of these cases did anyone touch an object in orbit. The attackers went for the vendor, the terminal, the management plane," Recorded Future explained.

Even as geopolitical rivalries fuel a new space race, the basics remain broken. "Every satellite has a terrestrial address: the ground stations that command it, the links that carry its telemetry, the user terminals at the edge, and the software supply chain behind it all. That is where attackers go, because that is where the doors are," according to the firm.

Its report dovetails with research by teams at the University of California, San Diego, and the University of Maryland. Using a satellite dish costing just $800, the researchers found that roughly half of the geostationary satellites they could observe were transmitting data unencrypted. The exposed traffic included telecommunications backhaul, corporate communications, and military data.

The US National Security Agency has also warned of the expanding attack surface created by the proliferation of low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellite networks. In a joint advisory with the Australian Signals Directorate and other international partners, the NSA examined security risks across the satellite communications ecosystem. This included satellites, ground stations and control centers, user terminals, end-user devices, radio links, and third-party suppliers. The agencies highlighted threats ranging from radio-frequency jamming, signal spoofing, and interception to weaknesses in ground infrastructure and user equipment.

Related:Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering

"The ground segment is highly exposed to cyber threats due to its extensive connectivity with terrestrial networks," the NSA and its partners warned. "Ground segments are typically the most interconnected and vulnerable points in a space system." Highlighted risks included malware injection, social engineering, DoS attacks, identity-based attacks, and poor user practices.

To address these risks, the advisory recommended continuous monitoring of ground systems, stronger endpoint security and access controls, and technical safeguards such as frequency-hopping signals, backup communications paths, and anti-jamming antennas to protect satellite links.

Recorded Future's own recommendations are for all stakeholders to begin treating space infrastructure as critical national infrastructure, holding vendors to stronger security standards, and implementing basic measures like encryption for satellite communication.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9632. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#9631. Same Product, Different Price: What an AI Shopping Agent Learned From 24,394 Items

Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.

Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.

Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.

Finding prices is easy. Proving two listings are the same product is the hard part.

Ask any AI shopping agent to find the best price and it will happily return one. The harder question is whether that price is for the same thing. A vacuum listed at two stores can differ by model year, bundle or pack size, and a price comparison that misses that is worse than none at all.

Deal.ai, an AI shopping agent built by Famous Labs, has been measuring both problems: how much prices really differ for identical products, and how hard it is to know two listings are identical in the first place.

From October 29 to November 4, 2026, Deal.ai compared 24,394 new products sold at two or more of 16 major U.S. retailers, including Amazon, Walmart, Target and Best Buy. Each store's price had to be read within an hour of the others.

The results were consistent. About two in three products had prices at least 5% apart across the big retailers. Among the 4,684 products sold at four or more retailers, a shopper who checked one store picked at random paid, on average, 15.6% above the lowest listed price. Checking two stores cut that to 7.4%, three stores to 3.7%, and four to 1.1%.

The biggest names were not always cheapest. At the same moment, another big retailer listed the item for less 37% of the time for Walmart products, 34% for Amazon, 41% for Best Buy and 51% for Target.

Those numbers only mean something if every price is for the same item. Deal.ai's answer is to separate matching from pricing.

In a live recheck on November 5, Deal.ai drew 600 products at random and kept the ones with a brand and a model number or barcode. A separate AI model then read each store's own listing title, with prices hidden, and kept only listings that were the identical item: same model, size, capacity, pack count and generation. Colour could differ; bundles, refurbished and open-box listings could not.

Of 4,990 store listings, 1,886 passed. That is a strict filter by design. It throws away near-matches that a looser system would happily compare, which keeps a "lower price" from really being a smaller pack or last year's model. Hiding prices from the matching model matters too: it stops the model from being swayed toward a match by a price that looks plausible.

"Finding prices is the easy part. The hard part is making sure every store is selling the exact same product, the same model and the same size," said Alex Mehr, Ph.D., co-founder and CEO of Famous Labs, the company behind Deal.ai. "That's what our agents are built to check, so shoppers can trust the price comparison they see."

Deal.ai puts that work behind a simple interface. Shoppers ask for what they want in plain English, and the agent researches the options, compares live prices across thousands of stores and sends them to the store with the best deal. Its agents also run every hour to surface unusually good deals, each with a deal score out of 10. A free deal checker takes a link to any deal and finds the same item at every big store.

For developers, Deal.ai also offers an MCP server, so other AI assistants can call it directly instead of scraping stores themselves.

Price data is abundant. Trustworthy comparisons are not. The gap between one store and the best price is large enough to matter to shoppers, but only if the agent is honest about which listings truly match. Strict matching, with prices hidden from the matcher, is a simple rule that makes every number after it more believable.

Deal.ai is free at deal.ai. The full study is published on Deal.ai's research page.

#9629. Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

This entry was posted on Tuesday 13th of October 2026 07:24 PM

One has to wonder how big the backlog of flaws is at this point. Maybe this month’s increase in the number of fixes just reflects an increasing number of people working on these fixes, and that they already have enough flaws to keep them all busy for a long time. Oh to be a fly on the wall.

Why do I still own and use a computer for my business?

For every invention, product, or process that man creates, several other problems are created for him. There never seems to be an end. I am glad that humans are actually testing the vulns that are discovered by LLMs, but for how long will that be the case? How long until the LLMs themselves well be checking there own vuln discoveries, testing and deploying with no human involvement…….

It comes down to basic Human Nature; biologically, we are still pretty much the same as our ancestors 0f 100,000 years ago. When the internet came along, what we did with it was pretty much what we did with nearly any new invention since then:

1. Get very excited about it 2. See if we could either: A. Stick it in our shorts B. See if it could be made a good weapon C. Amuse ourselves with it to the point of unconsciousness with it, or D. Enrich ourselves with it.

Unfortunately, ancient humans, when they picked up a rock, thought first about who they could bash over the head with it, not build a hospital.

I exaggerate a bit to make a point. We’ve come a little way since then, but that old hard-wiring is hard to erase. I imagine that, AI being made in our own image, will follow a similar course if not VERY strictly overseen.

Note: An old philosopher said that if we ever did produce something like an AI android, we would very shortly be very, very ashamed of ourselves.

I tend to disagree with the statement that the large number of CVE’s are placing strains on IT teams in terms of patch prioritization. That’s not the issue. For most vendors, Microsoft included, a single cumulative security update is issued, or a small handful for core products (Windows, Office, .Net). Whether those updates patch 100 or 10,000 individual CVE’s, the number of updates to test hasn’t really changed all that much. What HAS changed is the potential for the update to break things since more code is being modified with each update. Testing and deployment processes haven’t changed; it’s the monitoring for unexpected behavior during the testing phase that has become the pain point.

I agree. In my experience, for office workers, it’s low risk that patches will brake things. The factory floor is different. But even there, it’s not unusual to find PC’s running equipment not connected to the network due to the fact that they have to run proprietary software that won’t run on modern versions of Windows, or the PC-equipment interface is through a ISA or other legacy cards that modern versions of Windows do not support, and there is no way other than air-gapping to keep them secure. That’s why there are entire companies like NIXSYS (https://nixsys.com/) that build legacy computers using old CPU’s, old glue-chips & busses, and even old versions of Windows. No one junks a perfectly good but ancient CNC because it’s ancient PC died.

This was what I came here to say: it’s not the number of patches because everything gets rolled into one cumulative update. And Reguly is misinformed at best if he thinks IT teams can simply focus on the 26 most important updates – because we cannot select the 26 that are being exploited without also patching the CVEs that aren’t being exploited in the wild but for which the patch breaks, I don’t know, let’s say printing. Again.

So, what’s the patch record for Linux? search says patches published anywhere from 5~10 days after public notices are posted, not easy to match Microsoft’$ record…

Linux is starting to accept LLM vulnerability requests and they’re finding some flaws that have been around for decades. The total number is likely less, at least for the Linux kernel, but full distros use a large number of projects to create their OS and each of those pieces will have their own vulnerabilities.

See for example: https://security-tracker.debian.org/tracker/status/release/stable

That shows what’s currently being worked on for Debian. The first column notes the specific package the CVE refers to.

Should we call it a vulnerability if no attacker has any interest in it? I’m seeing a flood of vulns getting patched, but I’m not seeing a flood of vulns causing breaches…

If someone can make your mom stop, cry, and fork over a twenty to an animal shelter talking about puppies in a subway station, that is still a vulnerability of your mother, even if she is fortunate enough not to be approached on any one single given day of her daily commute.

#9628. DevOps Solved a Three-Variable Problem. AI Just Removed One of the Variables

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

DevOps was built on a trade-off. Ship code with speed, quality, and reliability, and accept that you're always balancing the three. Push too hard on speed and suffer the consequences in increased defects and downtime. Over-invest in review cycles and quality gates and shipping slows to a crawl. Every piece of the discipline we've built over the last fifteen years, CI/CD pipelines, the SDLC as most teams run it, sprint cadence, release process, exists to manage that three-way tension.

AI code generation has taken one of those three variables off the table. Code gets written fast now. That's no longer something a team has to actively manage or trade off against. It's a given.

Which means the balancing act DevOps was designed for doesn't exist anymore, at least not in its original form. Teams aren't weighing three things and searching for equilibrium. They're weighing two: quality and reliability. Speed has moved from a variable that must be optimized, to an assumed baseline.

That's a bigger shift than it sounds like. Most of the infrastructure of modern software delivery was built to manage a three-variable problem. If the problem has now become two-variable, the current infrastructure is set up for a constraint that is no longer present. Teams that keep gating releases the way they would if code-writing were still the bottleneck are optimizing for a problem they no longer have, while the two variables that actually matter now sit exactly where AI tools are weakest: making sure the code holds up in production, integrates cleanly with everything around it, and doesn't quietly degrade the system it lands in.

DevOps itself started as an attempt to solve a two-way split: the people who write code and the people who run it. Before DevOps, dev and ops were separate organizations with separate incentives, and the discipline existed to force them into one loop.

The fragmentation didn't stop there. It kept splitting, because no single person could hold the full context of a modern system in their head. So the work divided further: engineering writes the code, QA and testing verify it, SRE keeps it running, support and customer success handle what breaks in the field. Each team got its own tools to match: observability platforms, deployment pipelines, ticketing systems, support consoles, each built to serve one slice of the system because that's the most any team could realistically own.

That design made sense when writing code was the bottleneck and the constraint was human attention. Split the work, split the tooling, split the org, because there was too much for any one team to track.

AI code generation breaks that logic the same way it broke the speed variable. Engineers still write code, but writing it is no longer the scarce resource. The org structure and tooling built to protect people from too much context is solving a problem that's shrinking, while the actual bottleneck, quality and reliability across an increasingly AI-written system, is exactly what gets worse the more fragmented the teams and tools stay. Every silo boundary is a place context gets lost: QA doesn't have what SRE saw, support doesn't have what engineering shipped, and the AI helping one team doesn't know what the AI helping another team just decided.

Support, SRE, and QA were never really different problems. They're different interfaces onto one problem: how does this software actually behave. Support sees it through tickets. SRE sees it through incidents and infrastructure signals. QA sees it through tests and regressions. They split apart because no single system could hold all of that context at once. Now one system can.

That reframes what the emerging work of building shared context across support, SRE, QA and engineering. It isn't a sixth team added to the existing five. It's the work of building the thing none of those functions could build alone: a single connected model of how the system behaves in production, one that every function reads from and writes back into. A resolved ticket sharpens that model. A prevented escalation sharpens it. A traced incident sharpens it. Instead of five teams running five disconnected AI strategies, each starting from scratch on every interaction, one model gets smarter with every function that touches it, and every function benefits from what every other function already learned.

This is also why it compounds instead of just adding up. Give every function its own AI tool and you get faster, linearly, until the tool saturates. Unify those functions against one shared model and the hundredth incident gets cheaper to resolve than the tenth, because the system has already seen ninety like it. That curve isn't available to the fragmented version. Fragmented tools have no shared memory to compound against.

There's a version of this that just moves the silo one level down: a different AI agent for support, a different one for SRE, a different one for QA, each competent on its own, still not talking to each other. That doesn't solve the problem. It relocates it from teams to models.

What's actually needed sits above any individual agent or model. Not specialized to one task the way a single agent is, but tracking the continuity of a piece of work as it moves between people and agents, across roles, regardless of which model happens to be doing the work at any given moment. Less a better SRE agent, more the connective layer that remembers what happened, who or what handled it, and what was learned, no matter how many different tools touched it along the way.

This is the part that completes the picture. The org argument explains why the human silos need to dissolve. This is the same argument applied to the tooling: solve the org problem but leave every function running its own disconnected model, and the fragmentation just rebuilds itself one layer down.

None of this is about hiring a new team called AI Production Engineering and slotting it next to the other five. It's the recognition that support, QA, SRE, and engineering were always four surfaces on the same underlying problem, wired together by human handoffs because nothing else could do the wiring. Something else can now.

Speed took care of itself. The rethink is what the software development lifecycle looks like when quality and reliability are the only two levers left, and when the organizations and tools built to manage a human-attention constraint no longer need to hold that shape once the constraint is gone.

#9627. Latin America Sees Cyberattacks on Ports, Pipelines & Manufacturing

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

From the Port of Santos in Brazil to a pipeline in Argentina, cyberattacks are increasingly affecting industrial systems throughout the region.

On Nov. 6, a cyberattack encrypted data at the Port of Santos in Brazil, the largest port in South America. Around the same time, the data center serving the port suffered a power outage. The connection between the outage and cyberattack is still under investigation, but in combination, they affected the Santos Port Authority (APS) website, internal systems, and online services used by port customers.

The incident affected the APS enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems and services for customers on the website, which the organization just restored on Nov. 24, Paulo Silveira, a spokesman for the Port Authority, tells Dark Reading.

The incident was a ransomware attack, but the perpetrators remain unidentified, he says.

"The intruder was already in the systems and likely gained entry via a malicious email or by improperly accessing an infected website," he says. "The cyber-attack is under investigation, and the method of intrusion and the party responsible are still being traced."

Related:Cyprus Becomes Espionage Target for Iranian Hackers

The ransomware attack is the latest incident in a surge hitting industrial sectors in Latin America. In the third quarter, operations at several industrial facilities were disrupted by ransomware attacks, according to data published by cybersecurity vendor Dragos. While none of the attacks appeared to compromise an actual operational technology (OT) system — considered to be Stage 2 on the ICS Cyber Kill Chain — IT disruptions often cascade into operational problems, says Abdul Alamri, a principal threat intelligence analyst at Dragos.

"Often, ransomware groups do not need to reach OT to stop operations," he says. "When ransomware disrupts operations, it is usually through the enterprise IT, ERP and virtualization systems that operations depend on, or because the company shuts down production as a precaution."

Overall, cyber activity is ramping up in the southern hemisphere. While African nations have retaken the dubious honor of suffering the highest frequency of cyberattacks, Latin America is not far behind, with organizations in the region seeing an average of 3,483 per week, compared to Africa's 3,834 per week. The attacks are not just cybercriminals looking for opportunistic ransoms, but also nation-state threat actors aiming to compromise government and the private sector to gain intelligence on the politics in the region.

Many of the malicious incidents are ransomware. In the third quarter, industrial organizations in South America suffered at least 82 claimed ransomware incidents, up from 64 in the second quarter — the largest percentage increase of any major region, according to Dragos. Brazil topped the targeted nations with 22 incidents, while Peru and Argentina tallied 16 apiece, and Colombia saw 11 incidents, according to Dragos' Industrial Ransomware Analysis for Q3 2026 report.

Related:Nok et norsk energiselskap har blitt utsatt for et datainnbrudd på to dager

While Dragos tallies the number of victims claimed on ransomware groups' leak sites, Alamri considers the numbers to be conservative.

"We exclude victims we cannot identify or classify, and we remove victims that were already counted in an earlier quarter," he says. "Organizations that pay before they are posted never show up in the data."

Overall, organizations in Brazil, Mexico, and Argentina made up nearly two-thirds of ransomware victims, according to a second report, State of Cyber Threats 2026, published by Chilean telecommunications firm Entel Digital, which counts more than just industrial sectors.

In the Port of Santos incident, the cyberattack did not disrupt operations, mainly because the Santo Port Authority switched to alternate processes, says APS's Silveira. "The APS teams were working hard to attend to all the port users, assisted by e-mail, personal cellphones, and third-party systems," he says.

Related:Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in 2 Days

While the Port Authority managed to recover all their backups, they did suffer some loss of data after Oct. 31. APS is recovering that data from other records, Silveira says.

Similarly, an Argentinian pipeline company, Oldelval, suffered a cybersecurity incident that affected administrative systems, based on filings with the National Securities Commission (CNV), according to media reports. The attack did not hamper the movement of oil or crude, the company reportedly said.

While critical infrastructure is increasingly under attack, most global attacks on industrial firms target manufacturing, which also held true for South America this year; Dragos' Alamri says 57% of cyberattacks on industrial firms targeting the manufacturing sector.

Often, while OT systems are not compromised by a strict definition, they are still impacted. In past cases, incidents classified as IT-only cases actually affected engineering workstations and human-machine interface (HMI) hardware, which were classified as IT because they run Windows, he says.

"A statement that only administrative systems were affected can be accurate, and Oldelval reported that crude transport continued," he says. "However, these statements should be read with caution."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9626. U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering

The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”

The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

#9625. Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

In a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

Importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

(See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective)

When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:

Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error

Because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:

P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣

where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:

Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}

This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

What does FFF look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:

Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

We created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

To complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

We also released a more compact Python API:

HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

#9624. Why AI Agents Are Driving a New Kind of Database: OceanBase's Lakebase Approach

Artificial intelligence is moving beyond chatbots and content generation. Businesses are increasingly deploying AI agents that can retrieve information, analyze data, make decisions, and execute multi-step workflows. But as these applications become more sophisticated, an important limitation is becoming clear: traditional database architectures were not designed for all the demands of autonomous AI systems.

An AI agent may need to access real-time transaction records, analyze historical information, retrieve documents, interpret images, and maintain context throughout an interaction. Unlike conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications, agents may also need to maintain persistent state, update business records, execute transactions, and evaluate alternative courses of action. When this information is spread across disconnected systems, developers face additional integration work, data synchronization challenges, and operational complexity.

This raises an important question: Why do AI agents need an AI database designed around their requirements?

OceanBase, a distributed database provider with a background in mission-critical transaction processing, is addressing this challenge through its AI data infrastructure strategy, combining OceanLake, an integrated lakebase AI data platform, with OceanSeek, an open-source AI database designed for agents.

Traditional enterprise infrastructure generally separates transactional databases, analytical warehouses, and data lakes.

Databases manage operational records and real-time transactions. Warehouses support analytical workloads, while data lakes provide flexible storage for structured and unstructured information.

While technologies such as HTAP and data lakehouses have already begun to blur these boundaries, AI agents are accelerating this convergence.

Consider an AI agent working in a financial institution. It might need to retrieve customer transactions, analyze historical patterns, consult policy documents, and use business context before responding to a request.

If every information source resides in a separate environment, the application must coordinate multiple systems before the agent can complete its task.

This is why businesses are exploring AI agent infrastructure that brings operational data, analytics, and intelligent retrieval closer together.

OceanBase's lakebase approach combines the capabilities of databases, data warehouses, and data lakes within a unified architecture, building on its expertise in distributed transaction processing.

The objective is to support transactional processing, analytical computing, and flexible data storage without treating each workload as an entirely separate infrastructure problem.

OceanBase introduced OceanLake as an integrated lakebase AI data platform built around this concept.

OceanLake combines real-time transactional database capabilities, analytical computing, and open storage. It supports the unified management, processing, and retrieval of structured, semi-structured, and unstructured information.

This Llakebase integration is particularly relevant for AI applications because agents often need both current operational records and historical or contextual information.

A unified data foundation can simplify access to these resources and reduce the complexity of moving information between disconnected systems.

Enterprise information is no longer limited to rows and columns.

Documents, images, audio, video, and sensor data can contain valuable business information. As AI models become increasingly capable of processing these formats, organizations need infrastructure that can manage different information types together.

This is where multimodal fusion becomes important.

For example, an insurance application might need to combine customer records, policy documents, photographs, and historical claims to support an assessment.

OceanLake is designed to support structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data within a unified platform.

OceanBase has also reported multimodal data processing and model-training pipelines developed for Robbyant and LinkerBot.

The broader objective is to make enterprise information more accessible to AI applications rather than forcing developers to manage every data format independently.

AI agents require more than conventional database connectivity. They need efficient information retrieval, access to different data formats, and environments where developers can build and evaluate agent workflows.

OceanSeek is OceanBase's open-source AI database designed specifically for agent scenarios.

It adopts an integrated lakebase architecture, combining real-time database read/write and analytical capabilities with the open storage capabilities of a data lake.

Its supported capabilities include multimodal data management, hybrid retrieval, and data sandboxes.

Hybrid retrieval combines vector similarity search, full-text search, and structured data filtering. Data sandboxes leverage copy-on-write database and table forking, allowing agents to test operations and modify records without directly affecting production data.

For developers researching the best database for AI agents, these capabilities represent important evaluation criteria. The right choice depends on workload requirements, retrieval needs, data architecture, and deployment considerations.

Vector databases are another part of the broader AI data ecosystem, particularly for applications involving embedding-based retrieval. However, OceanSeek's positioning extends beyond a single retrieval capability by combining database, analytical, and multimodal data management functions.

The AI ecosystem is evolving rapidly. Developers are experimenting with different models, agent frameworks, and retrieval techniques.

Released under the Apache 2.0 license, OceanSeek allows developers to inspect, modify, and independently deploy the database.

OceanBase has open-sourced OceanSeek to encourage developers and industry partners to participate in building infrastructure for the agent era.

This approach gives the developer community another technology to explore as organizations build AI applications around their own data and operational requirements.

OceanBase's approach reflects four important priorities for modern AI infrastructure: lakebase integration, multimodal fusion, agent-friendliness, and open-source development.

OceanLake addresses the broader requirements of an integrated AI data platform, while OceanSeek focuses on the database capabilities needed for AI agents.

As enterprises move from AI experimentation toward production applications, the database is becoming more than a system for storing and retrieving records.

It is becoming a central part of AI agent infrastructure, helping connect business information with the intelligent applications that depend on it.

#9623. Cyber Insurers See New Divide: AI Defense 'Haves' & 'Have Nots'

Dark Reading Confidential Episode 23: Cyber insurers share their view of the AI-driven threat landscape and how mounting challenges are putting pressure on both sides of the policy, leaving the current model unsustainable.

Cyber insurance providers are approaching 2027 facing a fundamental challenge. Claims rose 40% in 2024 and another 20% in 2025, even as premiums have stayed largely flat. This trend is something both Coalition and Travelers say isn't sustainable; and at the center of that shift is AI, which is reshaping the threat landscape not by inventing new attack types, but by making existing ones — ransomware, business email compromise, and phishing — dramatically easier to execute at scale.

In this episode of Dark Reading Confidential, Dark Reading media and projects director Becky Bracken and Dark Reading senior news director Rob Wright sit down with Lauren Winchester, vice president of cyber-risk services at Travelers; and Daniel Woods, head of emerging risk at Coalition, to unpack what the data actually shows. The conversation moves past the headline-grabbing surge in disclosed vulnerabilities to a more nuanced picture: exploitation is rising, but not as sharply as disclosure volume, while AI-powered phishing kits are bring sold SaaS-style to criminals with little technical skill, driving a measurable spike in BEC and ransomware activity.

Related:How Southeastern University Got a Handle on Its Data

The two insurers also agree on where the real exposure lies: not necessarily with large enterprises, which have the resources to track threat intelligence and patch quickly, but with small and mid-sized businesses that often lack an in-house IT team altogether. That awareness gap, they argue, is where insurers now have to step in — not just to underwrite risk, but to actively help policyholders defend their organizations against it.

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please listen to the podcast or watch the video.

Dark Reading's Becky Bracken: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Dark Reading Confidential, a podcast from the editors of Dark Reading, where we bring you real-world stories straight from the cyber trenches. My name is Becky Bracken. I'm an editor with Dark Reading, and I am thrilled today to do just that: deliver as promised, along with my colleague Rob Wright. Today we are going to be talking about all things cyber insurance and AI. In addition to my very smart colleague Rob Wright, who I mentioned, we are thrilled to welcome Lauren Winchester, who is vice president of cyber risk services at Travelers Insurance, and of course Daniel Woods, who is the head of emerging risk at Coalition. Welcome to both of you. Thank you.

Related:US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise

DR's Becky Bracken: This conversation got started actually in one of our editorial meetings, and Rob had the smartest take, and then won the dubious distinction of getting to lead the conversation, which is always a problem around here when you have a smart idea. So, I am going to get out of the way and let Rob explain some of his very smart thinking around this topic, and get you guys in on it.

Dark Reading's Rob Wright: It wasn't a smart idea, but it was a question about what is happening with cyber insurance now that we have all this AI stuff going on. Thank you for joining me on this. We'll start with a basic question about where the cyber insurance industry is right now today in 2026, going into 2027. Just broad strokes. Ever since Project Glasswing, Mythos, and the tsunami of reported vulnerabilities, disclosed vulnerabilities, increases in zero-days. That's really put a lot of companies, a lot of vendors, and enterprises on the defensive. So, what effect is that having?

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: I think it's important not to conflate the surge in vulnerabilities being disclosed with a surge in attacks that drive cyber claims, at least not just yet. As many of your listeners will know, not all vulnerabilities are created equal, and so certainly there are thousands more vulnerabilities being disclosed in the months since Mythos preview came out, as compared to earlier in the year, and that's going to have an impact. And you have to look at the high-severity and the critical bugs within that group, and then you have to look at what's actually being exploited as well.

If we want to look at what's a good stand-in for exploitation, you can look at CISA's known exploited vulnerability list. There's a little lag there, but ultimately, if you look at the KEVs, you can see an increase that's happening, but it's not to the same order of magnitude as the overall CVE and vulnerability disclosure. But certainly, there is an increase. I think we just looked at this recently through Sept. 30, and CISA had added 246 KEVs in 2026, which exceeded the 245 added in total for 2025 when we looked at it. So naturally, we are on a trend to exceed last year.

We think maybe it'll be about a third more than last year, when we get to the end of the year, not a trend you want to see, but it's not in the same almost-exponential curve you're seeing with the total vulnerabilities. And I don't mean to be like everything's fine, right?

We also put out a report yesterday, and we look at ransomware leak site data as well as potential indicators of activity, and that's where ransomware threat actors are posting on their Dark Web leak sites who their victims are, and ultimately for Q3 2026, that activity was up. We had 111 distinct groups posting victims. We had a record number of 2,882 victims on leak sites, which is 26% up from the prior quarter and our highest quarter that we've ever seen. So certainly, the activity with the financially motivated threat actors is picking up, and we've also seen that in our business email compromises (BECs) as well, so it's painting a picture of more activity for sure. But just good to note that increased volumes don't necessarily mean increased tax immediately.

DR's Rob Wright: Gotcha. And I'll just say you are allowed to be positive on this podcast. I am going to actually implore you guys to give me some good news as we get deeper into this conversation because I always try to leave these discussions on a positive note, on a high note, rather than doom and gloom. So, we'll see if Daniel brings the doom and gloom now.

Coalition's Daniel Woods: So to bring a bit of gloom, I'd say the conversation also needs to look beyond just vulnerabilities and exploits. AI is a general-purpose technology, and it impacts not just the exploitation of vulnerabilities, but other mechanisms.

They were using AI to create convincing phishing lures, either by email or often replica websites. They would manipulate the user into letting the attacker in, even if MFA was enforced through either adversary in the middle and phishing, or device code phishing, and then the platform would get access to the mailbox, create mailbox rules, and start to pass through and identify sensitive data.

Travelers' Lauren Winchester: We see that in the ransomware ecosystem, where there's ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS), and so part of what we're looking for is when will the tools become even further identified, and to what extent, who will be doing that? Will it be the ransomware developers? How will that actually get disseminated into the ecosystem? There's a little bit more separation between the original, the victims, and who actually ends up doing the attack at the end, because of the access broker economy and what have you.
